about_movie: In a mist-shrouded futuristic city, an actor (Sophie Thatcher) and American soldier (Charles Melton) take on a supernatural killer with diamond-encrusted gloves who is murdering women.
review:
“People will say I’ve become unrelatable,” worries one character in Her Private Hell . This doesn’t feel like an anxiety that Danish filmmaker Nicholas Winding Refn has ever struggled with. He wasn’t especially relatable when making gritty crime dramas like Pusher and Bronson . His breakthrough film, the Ryan Gosling thriller Drive , deployed taciturn masculinity and ultraviolence alongside cool detachment. His work since then has become increasingly strange, held at a remove from the audience: from The Neon Demon ’s eye-swallowing fashion horrors to the pig-squealing sex scenes of Copenhagen Cowboy .

Her Private Hell — or to give it its full myopic title, Her Private Hell By NWR , taking auteur theory to exciting new levels of annoying — goes the furthest yet in the unrelatable stakes. Ostensibly, it’s another surreal, metaphysical, psychosexual fairy tale, the neon demons multiplied, an exercise less in style-over-substance than style-instead-of-substance. But more than any of his previous films, it feels like his lifelong quest for making challenging, aesthete-led art, unencumbered by convention or coherence, has finally run out of road.

As in Drive and The Neon Demon , Refn casts a doleful-looking young ingénue and subjects them to horrific violence and trauma. Here it is Gen-Z scream queen Sophie Thatcher; her character is a film star called Elle (a nod to Refn alum Elle Fanning?). We open in an eerie, misty-pink cityscape, the garish colours of Refn’s beloved giallo horrors immediately present. In the lobby of a vast hotel skyscraper, Elle meets a fan named Hunter (Kristine Froseth), and invites her to the well-appointed penthouse of her (wicked?) stepmother, Dominique (Havana Rose Liu).

There is talk of evil mist, and whispers of an otherworldly, serial-killing boogeyman called the Leatherman, whose face, we’re told, “is an infinite abyss”. Also in the mix, somehow, is Charles Melton’s Private K, an American GI: a strong, silent type out to exact vengeance for wrongs committed against women, yet who still finds time, in-between bloody beatings, to comb his impeccable hair.

It’s not that there isn’t a plot or characters here: there very much is, with a woozy love triangle of sorts, a gruesome revenge thread, and clear nods to the dark Hans Christian Andersen fable The Darning Needle . There are hints at a meta-narrative, too, a film about filmmaking: Elle stars in a hyper-stylised adaptation of a cheesy sci-fi comic book called Candy Floss, which plays as a kind of wanky fashionista Flash Gordon . “Making a movie is like going to war,” notes one character, suggesting this is Refn working through some stuff. But whether directly or indirectly, details are either fuzzy or ruinously incoherent. Mystery and ambiguity in filmmaking is always welcome, but the choices here feel just sloppy, patience-testing and childishly provocative. Often they simply don’t deliver; Dougray Scott’s Johnny Thunders is spoken of in whispered terms, yet disappears almost immediately.

Far more often — far too often — the female characters just seem like objects upon which to hang beautiful clothes and make-up, lining up to pose in straight-down-the-lens vignettes: as if props for a glamour magazine shoot, rather than living, breathing humans for a narrative. The male gaze is everywhere here, even if dressed in the veneer of female queerness. Refn’s camera smacks of Asian fetishism, too, a criticism he has fielded before in Only God Forgives .

What is it really about? The cycle of abuse? The Fall Of Man in boogeyman form? Something to do with mist? It’s never clear. Perhaps it makes sense to Refn. Across a two-hour runtime that feels like four, the film teeters precariously between the poles of captivating and insufferable, and too often lumbers into the wrong side.

Undoubtedly, Refn is a master stylist, and surrounds himself with master craftspeople. The production design by Gitte Malling is ambitious and imposing, a rare example of modern-day miniature work. The sound by Kristian Eidnes Andersen dials up the squeak of the leather and the crunch of the necks. The sweeping score from Pino Donaggio lends everything an operatic quality. The lurid palette of Magnus Nordenhof Jønck’s cinematography is jaw-dropping. Yet the finished product is just endlessly frustrating. The experience is akin to watching extremely beautiful paint dry. It would be obvious but not accurate to label this film as hell. Hell would be much less boring.
review_summary: Glossy nonsense. It’s dripping in style, and tries very hard to find the enigmatic cool to match, but Her Private Hell is just a very pretty load of old bollocks.

about_movie: When his son is abducted, widower Tom (Adam Scott) enlists his estranged ex-cop dad Pete (Robert De Niro) to help, along with Detective Amanda (Michelle Monaghan). Could the long-solved ‘Whisper Man’ murders be making a comeback?
review:
Many of the films produced under the Russo brothers’ AGBO banner feel – in a good way – like ‘90s throwbacks. 21 Bridges was a solid cop thriller elevated by the late, great Chadwick Boseman. Extraction was a solid hardman action movie elevated by the muscular Chris Hemsworth. The Whisper Man might not boast an MCU leading man, but it is – you guessed it – a solid serial killer thriller elevated by its star-studded cast.

The plot is nothing you haven’t seen before: a long-solved serial killer case of the ‘Whisper Man’ – who abducts emotionally-vulnerable young boys, with a nursery rhyme-esque ‘tapping at the glass’ mythology surrounding him – rears its head again many years later, when a new crop of kids start to go missing. The spree’s re-emergence coincides with emotionally shut-down widower Tom Kennedy (Scott) returning to his hometown, paying no attention to his son Jake’s (Acston Luca Porto) queries about seeing and hearing strange things in their new house. Before you know it, little Jake has been spirited away, sparking a quest to find him before he’s left for dead by… well, is it even the Whisper Man, since he’s firmly behind bars?

What heightens director James Ashcroft’s adaptation of Alex North’s novel is the eye-poppingly stacked cast. Jake’s disappearance causes Tom to reconnect with his distant detective dad Pete, a substantial role with which Robert De Niro imbues a baseline level of gravitas. The material hardly stretches him, but De Niro is – of course – extremely watchable in this kind of serious thriller fare. He is also believably cold in his relationship with Scott, their distance echoed in the survival-mode emotional wall Tom also displays to young Jake; running throughout The Whisper Man is a succession of broken father-son relationships, with ruinous results for all involved. Michelle Monaghan is handed a cookie-cutter role as the current cop on Jake’s case, but brings another dependable presence.

The juicier roles lie on The Whisper Man ’s more sinister side. Hamish Linklater, still in his post- Midnight Mass career boom, brings an eerie calm to murder-enthusiast Norman, his true crime obsession making him a prime suspect in the Whisper Man 2.0 killings. And Michael Keaton makes the most of limited screentime as the original Whisper Man, long locked away for his sick deeds, ready to play Hannibal Lecter-esque mind games with the police when they seek his advice on who might be picking up where he left off. An extended scene between Keaton and De Niro is the highlight here; two titans simply going head-to-head across a table.

There are no surprises to be found in The Whisper Man ; it isn’t destined to go down as a new classic of the genre. But with a cast this great, well-crafted tension, and just enough character meat on the bones, it’s a film that deserves neither whispers, nor shouts, but a regular-volume recommendation. May AGBO’s ‘90s throwback project long continue.
review_summary: A Netflix serial killer thriller that’s – whisper it! – actually pretty good, with a heavyweight cast that brings greater heft to solid if forgettable material.

about_movie: Twenty-three-year-old Elliot (Cooper Hoffman) becomes a sexual muse for his older provocateur boss Erika (Olivia Wilde).
review:
Gregg Araki’s first film in over a decade opens with chaos: a naked female body facedown in a pool and a terrified male onlooker in pink lingerie, nose bloodied. Sex and shock are on a par with oxygen in the cult filmmaker’s oeuvre — his ‘Teenage Apocalypse’ trilogy features suicide, the forcefeeding of a severed appendage and an abundance of boundary-crushing fornication. In 2026, however, the teens ain’t what they were, and Araki and his co-writer, sex journalist Karley Sciortino, have mined Gen Z’s tangled relationship with pleasure for their BDSM two-hander.

Taking the role of dom is Olivia Wilde’s Erika Tracy, a strikingly assembled artist-turned-floating-body. She hires Elliot (Cooper Hoffman), an aimless soul 14 years her junior, as an assistant. Told through flashbacks, with Elliot as a witness speaking to detectives Zola and Zem (Maggie Cho and Johnny Knoxville), we learn that a week into the job, Erika invites him to enter into a sexual relationship with her. Partly for her art, also for fun; the motivations aren’t dwelled upon, as Elliot’s hungry eyes can barely stay in his skull.

A kaleidoscope of coitus ensues, more screwball than sensationalist. Elliot crawls on the floor upon Erika’s command and splays out blindfolded, thirstily awaiting her touch. In no time he’s intoxicated, his tantalising second life a tonic compared to his modest houseshare and uninterested girlfriend Minerva (Charli xcx, an eye-roll in human form). He bears all the surface traits of a modern, liberal young man: a “Forever Feminist” laptop sticker, a shabbiness that feels part-accidental, part-curated. Yet Hoffman makes him an open book: earnest, charming, and easy for even the icy Erika to warm to. In a sweet, stolen moment, Wilde slides her thumb into Hoffman’s mouth while he sits on her lap, her fingers gently stroking his beard.

Erika is assigned little backstory but Wilde knows when to give a little more and when to take even more away. What few personal breadcrumbs Erika dispenses Elliot devours, hoping the trail will lead to a steady relationship. It’s predictable yet understandable: on his podcast he describes his generation’s “conflicted and confusing” feelings about sex, amplified by the pandemic. Erika is all answers in a world of overwhelming questions (Elliot even has “Yes?” and “No?” tattooed above his knuckles). I Want Your Sex , alas, is hung up on the questions. The mystery of the opening scene drives the story towards a spirited but ambiguous conclusion, instead of burrowing further down the kinky rabbit hole. Yet a somewhat stilted end to the dynamic doesn’t undo the fizz and thrills that have come before.
review_summary: A rallying cry for the young, insecure and horny that doesn’t reach a wholly satisfying climax. But, bolstered by a magnetic Cooper Hoffman, this still has plenty of bang for your buck.

about_movie: Lawyer Rachel Wild (Eiza González), alongside her specialist fixers Sid (Henry Cavill) and Bronco (Jake Gyllenhaal), specialise in recovering debts for the ultra-rich, by any means necessary. Have they met their match in taking on billionaire gangster Manny Salazar (Carlos Bardem)?
review:
Is there any studio director working today as prolific as Guy Ritchie? In the last ten years, the British filmmaker has made an astonishing nine feature films, including two huge war movies, a gangster feature, and a billion-dollar-grossing Disney blockbuster , not to mention shepherding four major television shows to the small screen. His latest film — arriving in the same month as new seasons of MobLand and The Gentlemen , for which he has directed several episodes — is hardly a small back-to-basics indie affair. It’s a grand, globe-trotting, action-heavy adventure with explosions and setpieces galore. The man is a machine.

If there’s a sense — as is also the case with Ritchie’s sometime collaborator Jason Statham — that the director has Made His Film Again, that charge does not feel unfounded here. Like The Ministry of Ungentlemanly Warfare or Operation Fortune: Ruse de Guerre , it has a caper-ish tone and a goofy approach; like his earlier geezerish efforts Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels and Snatch , it’s high on laddy bants and alpha male energy. Yet our protagonist here is an unusual one for a Ritchie hero: a pen-pushing lawyer, and rare female presence in his normally very blokey work, albeit a woman surrounded almost entirely by very blokey characters.

As she explains to us in an overwritten narration, Rachel Wild (Eiza González) is a no-nonsense lawyer who exists in the grey of the title, operating in the area between what is strictly legal and what is not. She works with ultra rich clients plucked from the 1% of the 1% — this is obviously not the film to explore themes of global wealth inequality — in order to recover assets in the billions. Rachel’s firm uses all kinds of tactics at their disposal: from clever legal pressures to those of the more bang-bang-shoot-shoot variety. For the slightly more off-the-books stuff, she hires her trusted fixers, the colourfully named Sid (Henry Cavill) and Bronco (Jake Gyllenhaal), who have teams which specialise in “extraction, intimidation, and sabotage,” and “corruption, bribery and covert surveillance”, respectively.

Despite featuring a plot about the strategic deployment of extrajudicial legal mechanisms exerting pressure on debtors, this is no slow-burn Grisham-esque potboiler. Indeed, it has the trappings of a heist movie, with its playful score, glamorous locations, Q-branch-style gadgetry and best laid plans. One such scheme is presented to us while Rachel makes a ‘Stovetop Negroni Svegliato’, as on-screen titles helpfully inform us — just to emphasise how glossy and chic and exciting this legal work is.

As with many heist films, it is all exposition and barely anything in the way of character; Cavill and Gyllenhaal are given free rein to run on charm autopilot (all we learn of Sid is that his nickname is ‘Captain Sensible’) while Rachel is just straightforwardly competent, almost never making a mistake. There is one scene where the gang get into a bit of jeopardy but Ritchie’s script (he is the only credited writer, his first sole screenwriting credit in nearly 20 years, since 2008’s RockNRolla ) is too enamoured with these slick, sexy characters to let them get into harm’s way. They simply plan for every eventuality to recover their money from scowling ’80s-era baddie Salazar (Carlos Bardem), and absolutely do so.

Is it nonsense? Of course it is. Is it predictable? Almost entirely. Is it funny? Not really, except in a slightly try-hard manner. Is it even remotely memorable? Not in the slightest. Does it plod along at a jolly old pace, with muscular action setpieces and a runtime that doesn’t outstay its welcome? It’s a Guy Ritchie film. Of course it does.
review_summary: A typically bro-y action affair, even with its nominal female lead, this is standard-issue Ritchie: a filmmaker who has found a comfortable niche in the watch-in-the-background streaming era and shows no sign of changing. Does the job.

about_movie: Digger Rockwell (Tom Cruise), a billionaire oil tycoon, has his life thrown into disarray when one of his oil plants causes a potentially apocalyptic disaster.
review:
Alejandro González Iñárritu has often been a polarising filmmaker. Depending on your view, his style is either bravura technical audacity or pure indulgence. At his best, his wild trickery amplifies compelling characters. Birdman 's single shot echoes a man’s inability to escape himself. The Revenant 's relentless bloody chaos reflects the savagery of a man’s life, inside and out. One of many frustrating things about Digger is that all Iñárritu’s exquisite staging and narrative Russian doll-ing aren’t in service of anything particularly effective. The presentation is challenging but Digger doesn’t dig very deep.

Iñárritu kicks us into his film like a boot from behind. The titular character, an elderly oil tycoon played by Tom Cruise encased in prosthetics from balding head to bum crack, is roused from bed by an urgent call. Within minutes, one of Digger’s Arctic oil fields has ruptured, an iceberg named Judy is on her way to decimate Scandinavia, the US President’s on the phone, and the end of the world looks distinctly possible. There’s no time to steady yourself. The dizzying momentum continues as Digger (sort of) tries to avert Armageddon.

This becomes wearing rather than exciting because there’s nobody for us to grip onto as we hurtle along. We’re as adrift as Judy amid a sea of characters with little interior life. Digger is a bumptious blowhard. A fantastic supporting cast — Sandra Hüller, John Goodman, Jesse Plemons — each play a single note. Only Riz Ahmed, as a conflicted scientist who could have bumbled in from a Wes Anderson picture, has any dimension. An early meta twist tries to give the story some grounding and explain away the cartoonishness, but it doesn’t entirely make sense, even by its own logic, and functions mostly as a way for Iñárritu to comment on his own work. This is the film’s chief problem— that it appears more concerned with itself than with the audience. Its apparent message — that the planet’s dying and we’re complicit, as much as we crave villains to blame — is delivered in almost hectoring terms, often in loud monologues. For a film about the complexity of mankind , it shows scant interest in actual people.

If the whole isn’t successful, elements are. Emmanuel Lubezki’s cinematography and Dennis Gassner’s production design achieve the Kubrickian grandeur Iñárritu clearly intends. Cruise emerges with a win, reminding us how riveting he can be as an actor, not just as a movie star. A role so oversized and absurd demands fearless commitment , which he certainly gives. The big swing is laudable. If only the film were more rewarding.
review_summary: Visually impressive, and Cruise gives his all. But Digger doesn’t have much going on beneath the surface. A disappointing waste of a superb team.

movie_name_try2: Call My Agent! The Movie Review
about_movie: Five years after her agency ASK’s collapse, former agent Andréa (Camille Cottin) is directing her first film when her leading man quits and she fires her producer. Desperate to save the production, she recruits former assistant Noémie (Laure Calamy) and attempts to recast the film and avert disaster.
review:
Making a movie about a TV show about the monstrous egos behind movies and television risks disappearing up your own satirical arse. Add a litany of cameos, including George Clooney as George Clooney and Eva Longoria as, you guessed it, Eva Longoria, and Call My Agent! The Movie sounds like a true over-indulgent meta nightmare. But this long-awaited sequel to the beloved TV series remains, against the odds, rather delightful.

Directing her debut feature, Andréa (Camille Cottin) discovers that managing a production is harder when you can’t simply make demands at increasing volume down the phone until everyone falls in line. With her leading man gone and the shoot in peril, she drafts in her former assistant turned reality-TV producer Noémie (Laure Calamy), while genial agent Gabriel (Grégory Montel) and the rest of ASK are also gradually dragged into the chaos.

Director Émilie Noblet, working from a screenplay co-written by series creator Fanny Herrero, has fun reversing the old power dynamic. Andréa, once charged with placating impossible filmmaker egos, has become one herself. Her increasingly desperate attempts to keep her film alive supply pleasing karmic retribution, while old resentments ensure the ASK reunion is hardly a warm group hug. The feature format inevitably loses some of the series’ nimble episodic rhythm, particularly as the crises pile up, but its refusal to treat any of this showbiz nonsense as terribly important keeps the self-indulgence largely at bay.

Cottin remains magnificent, with her Andréa capable of turning even a plea for help into an implied threat. Motherhood may have somewhat softened her, but she hasn’t been defanged. Watching this fierce consummate control freak discover that directing actually requires some diplomacy gives the film its sharpest comic edge. While the cameos occasionally threaten to tip it into Hollywood navel-gazing, they are thankfully fleeting enough to just remain fun asides. Call My Agent! The Movie is naturally more indulgent at feature length, but its barbs remain sharp enough to skewer any pomposity.
review_summary: A potentially insufferable showbiz victory lap instead proves a witty, affectionate reunion for our favourite French talent agents. It’s occasionally indulgent and less nimble than the beloved series, but Camille Cottin remains excellent throughout.

about_movie: New York poet Ed Saxberger’s (Willem Dafoe) passion for writing is rekindled when a group of young admirers rediscover him, though he’s particularly charmed by the society’s only woman, flirtatious actor/singer Gloria (Greta Lee).
review:
Willem Dafoe has a reputation for weird and wacky performances, from Poor Things , The Lighthouse and Nosferatu stretching all the way back to Wild At Heart . So it’s disarming to see him inhabit a role so rooted in normalcy. In critic-turned-filmmaker Kent Jones’ low-stakes drama, Dafoe plays ageing New Yorker Ed Saxberger, once a promising poet, now an unassuming post-office worker sorting the writing of others while his pen lies dormant.

A chance meeting with Wilson Meyers (Edmund Donovan), a young writer with ambition bursting out of his turtleneck, leads Saxberger to The Enthusiasm Society, a group composed of sprightly writers (read: New York nepo babies). They become his devoted disciples as they excitedly plan a recital where he can premiere new material. However, his attention is drawn to flamboyant actor/singer and self-described ingénue Gloria Gardener (Greta Lee). The subtlety of Dafoe’s grounded performance clashes beautifully with Lee’s flirtatious theatricality; she sidesteps Manic-Pixie-Dream-Girl cliché with wonderfully sarcastic declarations: “There is nothing more exciting than a rediscovered male genius.” Though she has two impressive set-pieces, you can’t help but crave more screen time for Lee and her velvety croon.

Samy Burch comfortably adapts Arthur Schnitzler’s posthumously published 1895 novella for contemporary New York, while Jones frames dialogue as if it’s poetry, with staccato back-and-forth cuts before still shots imitating a breath between stanzas. Still, as Late Fame settles into its lyrical rhythm, following Saxberger as he roams the streets with acute familiarity, Dafoe’s poetic voice-over does teeter towards the sentimentality that it satirises.

Jones flits between Saxberger’s “lowbrow” pool-bar pals and lowlight literary events without judgement. Saxberger’s writer’s block, Meyers’ snobbery and Gardener’s aspiration are all regarded with dignity. Even the film’s conclusion, a sort of unflashy anti-climax, feels wise; like a ruminative line of meaningful poetry that lingers in the silence.
review_summary: Willem Dafoe’s stripped-back performance is a compelling treat in this low-key but moving intergenerational portrait of ambitious writers.

about_movie: Hank (Alan Ritchson) works in Brisbane as a ‘runner’, a sort of glorified delivery man making drops that might be sensitive or dangerous. When he’s sent to pick up a human organ and its courier Ben (Owen Wilson), he finds himself the target of murderous goons.
review:
When the universe closes a season of Reacher , it opens a window — with Runner . This enjoyable slice of mindless high-concept action nonsense allows star Alan Ritchson to once again brood, punch and blow things up. Ritchson has considerably more range than is on display here, but what this lacks in originality it makes up for in pace and effectively delivered mayhem.

Our hero is delivery man Hank Malone, a US immigrant to Brisbane who’s rebuilding his life after war, trauma and tragedy. One day, he’s tasked with transporting a human organ, newly arrived by private jet, to its recipient — but it turns out that the organ and its courier, Ben Bishop (Owen Wilson), are the target of ne’er-do-wells who are determined to get hold of it at any cost. Hank, who unsurprisingly has a military background, must keep Bishop and the package safe. Cue carnage up and down the Gold Coast as Rodrigo Santoro’s vaguely defined cartel boss Dámian Zaldívar and his interchangeable army of biker-gang minions attempt to get their hands on the precious liver.

It’s honestly an inspired MacGuffin for a big, dumb action movie, and the movie regularly reminds us of the stakes by cutting away to Leila George’s instantly sympathetic Kate, mother to a very sick little girl. Director Scott Waugh also takes just enough time to establish some broad-strokes character for Hank and Ben. The former, naturally, is taciturn, determined and hiding pain beneath gruff loneliness; the latter is all charm and chat and ill-equipped to deal with near-death experiences. It’s an (overly) familiar dynamic, but one that is still dependable, and Ritchson gives Hank enough wounded charm that he doesn’t get too formulaic — even if he does make the Reacher-ish claim that, “I am not someone people successfully fuck with.”

Much of the action involves car chases weaving in and out of suspiciously disciplined civilian traffic, Waugh’s camera (and VFX) swooshing around them, but there’s a surprisingly high body-count for a film ostensibly about saving a life and some wince-inducingly crunchy kills. Still, that’s what we came for, and who cares when they’re faceless goons trying to kill a small child? It’s all just grist for the mill — and hopefully the desperately ill people of Brisbane will have a few more organs available after all of this.
review_summary: It's business as usual for both Ritchson and Wilson, but perfectly serviceable action baloney with just enough humour and emotion to keep you engaged.

about_movie: Three days before D-Day, Chief Meteorological Officer James Stagg (Andrew Scott) informs General Dwight D. Eisenhower (Brendan Fraser) that the military operation should be delayed.
review:
If 100 minutes of weather chat sounds like your idea of hell, then feel the Pressure . A well-mounted, extremely efficient World War II thriller, this latest from director/co-writer/editor Anthony Maras delivers an absorbing lesson in filmic forecasting, as the fate of the free world seesaws on the vagaries of wind speed, precipitation, cloud cover and visibility levels. The result is a comfy old-school pot-boiler — at one point there is a literal ticking clock — anchored by the ever-brilliant Andrew Scott on tip-top form.

Based on David Haig’s 2014 play, Pressure is essentially a chamber piece set in the Allied military HQ in the run up to D-Day. We are shadowing meteorological expert James Stagg (Scott), a dour Scot deemed a “genius” by Churchill, who is brought in to assess whether the weather conditions are suitable for Operation Overlord. Reporting to General Dwight D. Eisenhower (Brendan Fraser), it’s a case of cloudy with a chance of meatheads as the military establishment — including Damian Lewis’ Field Marshal Montgomery — refuse to hear Stagg’s prognosis that the weather is too inclement to launch. It’s an all too resonant take on powerful Americans rejecting expertise.

Soon Stagg is locking horns with American meteorologist Irving Krick (a slick-ass Chris Messina), Eisenhower’s right-hand weatherman who once predicted the conditions on the Gone With The Wind set. Krick relies on historical weather patterns. Stagg believes in science, fresh data and informed guesses. There’s tons of fun to be had in the two men battling for the ear of Eisenhower, a quiet new guy treading on the established loudmouth’s toes.

If this is competency porn of the highest order, Scott is its Dirk Diggler. The actor never makes Stagg likeable or sympathetic; instead, he is uptight but magnetic, his subdued personality underpinned by a bedrock of integrity and conviction. In a career full of highs, this is another stand-out. In some respects, given Scott’s subtlety, Fraser feels like he is in a different movie. His Eisenhower is a larger-than-life figure — like the weather, big and blustery — although he finds moving moments expressing his doubts about the invasion. He is well matched by Kerry Condon as his personal secretary. As in The Banshees Of Inisherin and F1 , she is the gal among the guys, adding common sense and emotional weight amid all the testosterone.

When it comes to D-Day, Maras works wonders meshing staged combat action with wonderfully restored archive footage. But Pressure ’s pleasures are mostly cerebral, smart people figuring stuff out under extraordinary duress. It’s so gripping, even your dad might stay awake.
review_summary: Led by a stellar Andrew Scott, Pressure is a conventional but compelling look at a little-known vignette from the theatre of World War II. Small, smart and perfectly formed.

about_movie:
Schoolteacher Maria’s (Saoirse Ronan) class is routinely disrupted by one
troublesome pupil. She takes extreme measures to restore peace.
review:
The plight of a teacher is an unenviable one: kids can be real demons sometimes. As the perennial saying goes, one bad apple spoils the bunch —and in the case of poor primary-school educator Maria ( Saoirse Ronan ), that piece of unsavoury produce is Danny (Eddie Waller), a violent brat whose unruly outbursts have rendered her classroom a place where chaos reigns. This is the English-language feature debut of Swedish filmmaker Jonatan Etzler, and as delicious as his biting satire of Britain’s education system is, it’s astutely aware of the brutal realities of working as a teacher. Maria has well-intentioned hopes of enriching young minds, but all of her time is occupied by managing one problem child. The school’s headteacher is uncaring towards her struggles — never mind the helicopter parents who have a word or ten to say about their child’s education.

When one particular incident involving Danny leaves another pupil with a broken bone, Maria decides to take matters into her own hands in ways no curriculum would ever recommend. In the first of the film’s many entertaining, demented turns, Danny winds up trapped in Maria’s dingy basement, for one-on-one specialised education. When Danny fails to show up to school, however, she finds students, faculty and parents alike breathe a collective sigh of relief.

That her entire town would rather turn a blind eye to a problematic child’s disappearance than address the root structural causes of the issue reflects the cleverness of the razor-sharp if unsubtle script by screenwriter Jess O’Kane. (If the title’s fruitful metaphor wasn’t already clear, an opening scene at an apple-harvesting plant draws that connection almost too plainly.) Beneath the political commentary is a riotous comedy, laugh-out-loud hilarious precisely because of the unbelievable lengths the film dares to go.

By the fever-pitch third act, Bad Apples ' leaps in logic might test your suspension of disbelief. But Ronan keeps it all tethered to the real world. It’s rare these days to see the actor outside of period dress, and it’s refreshing and exhilarating to see her in comedic mode. Her character’s frustration and desperation radiates from her, but there’s an earnestness to Maria that keeps her sympathetic — even as she makes one calamitous decision after another. As much as she blatantly crosses the ethical line, Maria just wants the best for her students.

It helps that Ronan has a pair of brilliant young scene partners by her side: newcomer Waller is terrifying as Danny, who masks a gentle side beneath his rage. Nia Brown is just unnerving as Pauline, a teacher’s pet whose eagerness to please threatens to derail Maria’s plans. Bad Apples gets to the rotten core of modern Britain, but the absurdity of it all makes you want to take bite after bite.
review_summary: Jonatan Etzler’s school satire is darkly hilarious and politically sharp — as satisfying as a crisp Granny Smith. Saoirse Ronan has never been better walking its riveting moral tightrope.

about_movie: When the Owens family curse strikes again, Kylie (Joey King) travels to England seeking a cure, with her mother Sally (Sandra Bullock) and aunt Gillian (Nicole Kidman) in hot pursuit.
review:
Witch stories have always had a particular feminist power. Whether antagonists or protagonists, the best witches embody feminine rage and possibility, women refusing the limits imposed upon them. Perhaps that explains the glut of belated revivals of millennial witchy touchstones, from The Craft to Hocus Pocus . For many of us, these were the women who raised us. Unfortunately, resurrection is a tricky business. Practical Magic 2 , while hardly an abject failure, joins the pile of witchy sequels perhaps better left burned at the stake.

Twenty-five years on, the Owens family faces another crisis when Kylie (Joey King), daughter of Sally (Sandra Bullock), falls for dreamy Gideon (Xolo Maridueña), only for the family curse to put him in a coma. Kylie heads to England seeking a cure, pursued by sisters Sally and Gillian (Nicole Kidman), who seek help from sexy magic academic Ian Wright (Lee Pace) — sadly not that Ian Wright, which might have been cool.

There are pleasures to be found here. The glittering jewel-toned aesthetic, Stevie Nicks-inspired costuming and commitment to aspirational fairy-tale architecture remain a joy, as does reuniting Sally, Gillian, Frances (Stockard Channing) and Jet (Dianne Wiest). Even saddled with woeful dialogue and plot machinations that literally could have been an email, these formidable actors remain enchanting presences, and their gentle teasing and bickering is where the film feels the most alive. King rises gamely to the occasion, while Maisie Williams is squandered, largely wandering about with an inauspicious ’90s-prom updo.

More disappointing is how male-centred and heteronormative this return feels. The original understood romantic love was only one ingredient in the potion; its real fantasy lay in sisters, aunts and daughters building a strange, unruly world together. Decades later, when women, witches and sequels can be anything, it’s dispiriting to find so little imagination in what their lives might become.
review_summary: The Owens women remain bewitching company, but this belated sequel trades the original’s unruly feminist magic for something disappointingly conventional. The midnight margaritas are back. The magic, sadly, isn’t.

about_movie: Elinor (Daisy Edgar-Jones) and Marianne (Esmé Creed-Miles) Dashwood, two very different sisters, navigate the passion and pitfalls of first love.
review:
Hitch up your petticoats: it’s Austen autumn. Later this year, we’ll get a Netflix miniseries of Pride And Prejudice , but first up is this achingly tasteful take on Jane Austen’s other big-hitter, Sense And Sensibility . It’s the first feature film adaptation of the story since Ang Lee’s movie back in 1995 , which boasted an Oscar-winning script by Emma Thompson.

You can imagine the trepidation of director Georgia Oakley, who broke out with 2022’s lesbian drama Blue Jean , and debut screenwriter Diana Reid, to approach this hallowed material. And while there are some flourishes that help make the story feel contemporary (the eternal mission of the period-drama filmmaker), sadly the film struggles to carve out its own distinct identity, feeling more like a hotchpotch of influences than a unique retelling.

Wisely, Oakley opens the film by emphasising that the real subject underpinning every Austen novel is women’s lack of economic security. The Dashwood sisters, reserved Elinor (Daisy Edgar-Jones), passionate Marianne (Esmé Creed-Miles) and tomboyish Margaret (Bodhi Rae Breathnach), are being turfed out of their stately home thanks to wills always favouring sons over daughters. Elinor finds a kindred spirit in Edward Ferrars (George MacKay), the kindly and shy brother of scheming in-law Fanny (Stacy Martin). Their early scenes together are the film’s best, with Edgar-Jones and MacKay building a warm, tender rapport, and MacKay making Edward come across as principled and loyal, rather than a wet blanket.

But the Dashwoods are soon shipped off to the only home they can now afford, a small cottage in Devon, where Marianne falls into the arms of the devilishly charming John Willoughby (Frank Dillane), to the chagrin of strong but silent Colonel Brandon (Herbert Nordrum).

It certainly all looks ravishing, the 35mm film stock beautifully capturing the textures of the natural world in which the sisters frolic. But the cinematography, costumes and production design seem heavily indebted to Joe Wright’s 2005 Pride And Prejudice , with some overt references to Wuthering Heights and Far From The Madding Crowd . Having grappled with Austen’s key themes, the film’s focus shifts to straightforward romance, which feels rather played out and, crucially, not especially funny.

Edgar-Jones holds the fort, but the central relationship between the two sisters with such opposing attitude too love also feels rather underserved, as if the screenplay’s expansion of the central romantic relationships ironically means the sacrifice of the story’s real heart.
review_summary: Bolstered by strong performances, this handsome but derivative take is a little bloodless, with Austen’s sharp wit sanded down to fit a more romantic mould.

about_movie: Following the events at the B67 TV Tower, Jax (Harriet Slater) and Luce (Arsema Thomas) climb to the top of Thailand’s Mount Kwan — with disastrous results.
review:
2022’s Fall was a ruthlessly efficient genre exercise, stripping the disaster-survival thriller down to its most essential parts. The premise was simple: two climbers (Grace Caroline Currey’s Becky and Virginia Gardner’s Shiloh), one grieving the loss of her husband, the other a devil-may-care YouTuber, accidentally get trapped on the top of America’s tallest TV tower, and must use their wits and ingenuity to escape.

This minimalist but highly effective B-movie was a sleeper hit in the Covid era, so it has spawned a second go-around. Echoing the first film’s surprise success, the original climbers are now social-media stars, with thousands of “Fall-owers”, as one podcaster puts it — but our heroes this time are Jax (Harriet Slater), the younger sister of Shiloh, and Shiloh’s friend Luce (Arsema Thomas). They find Shiloh’s journal with an ambitious climbing bucket-list, and Luce convinces Jax to traverse the treacherous plank walk of Thailand’s Mount Kawn — which has, at its summit, the ‘Death Dragon’, a statue said to eat your fears.

Like the first film, this is a very basic story about facing your phobias, about characters dealing with the grief of a climbing tragedy by brazenly inviting a new one. Like the first film, the only true antagonists here are rusty screws rattling out of place, the hundreds of metres below their feet, and the unstoppable power of gravity. And just like the first film, it is at its best when giving you the absolute willies.

There are so many moments where these characters could, and should, just say: “Nope!” Ladders wobble. Signs warn of extreme danger. Risk assessments are nonexistent. Soon they get stuck on something called the Devil’s Elbow. Then it starts pissing it down — couldn’t they have checked the forecast? — and our plucky heroes are contending with thunderstorms, earthquakes, landslides, even drug cartels. It’s not just heights that will trouble you now.

One particular sequence, in which the pair swing on monkey bars — with no rope! — at 3,000 feet will make you squirm. Yet while it is brutally effective in the sweaty-palm department, it somewhat falters elsewhere. Very basic dialogue (“We are going to make it out of here!”), simplistic character development (getting stranded on a mountain will help conquer your fears!) and cheesy backstories (one core childhood memory is conveniently recorded on a camcorder) makes the experience feel scrappier and more generic than its sharply drawn predecessor.

Still, in the disaster-thrills department, it does the job. And in its final moments, it makes an audacious gamble for franchise expansion (the FCU?) with a very confident sequel tease. Will we soon see our heroes team up to battle gravity itself?
review_summary: Not quite as direct a hit of adrenaline as the first film, but still a compelling argument against ever climbing any higher than sea level. Expect absolutely dripping palms.

about_movie: When the police are called regarding a situation involving an elderly couple, dementia and consent, the family at the centre of it find themselves engulfed in an increasingly painful and devastating set of circumstances.
review:
The first time we see Anna Calder-Marshall’s Leslie and Tom Courtenay’s Martin, it is from the back. Even so, you can feel the mutual compassion, the love, the support, this old married couple hobbling up some steps together, arm in arm, her gripping the bannister, him grasping a walking stick. For an opening shot, it does a lot of heavy lifting. An uphill struggle? You bet.

When we next see them, a couple of minutes later, another perspective, and another act of love. Seemingly. It is daytime in their modest north London house, and Leslie’s daughter Amanda (Juliette Binoche) walks in on them having sex. It’s a functional, humdrum sex scene – Leslie, in fact, looks practically lifeless. Amanda, distraught, lashes out at a sheepish Martin, her stepfather, reminding him that she’s told him again and again not to do this, that if he kept doing so, she would call the police. He objects, and she does just that.

As she explains to them on the phone, her mother has advanced dementia and doesn’t have the capacity to give sexual consent. They ask Amanda if she saw her struggling. “She doesn’t resist because she doesn’t know what’s happening to her,” she responds. And as the authorities get involved, so begins a chain of events shedding light on emotional ethical quandaries, and on a bureaucratic system doing its best under quite impossible circumstances. When SOIT (Sexual Offences Investigation Trained) officers decide to temporarily separate Martin and Leslie, Amanda objects. Leslie is completely dependent on Martin, she explains: “He loves her, dearly.”

This is a very upsetting film, an incisive investigation of a complex, thorny, and sorely human situation, in which binary offerings of what is morally right or wrong are not clear cut – how could they be, when even the person at the heart of it all may not know what they want? One of the most perplexing issues it explores is disinhibition, in which the person, because of the condition, runs on purely primal instincts. And they may well absolutely want sex with their partner. Should others be able to deny it of them – definitively, indefinitely – because they may not knowingly be consenting, even if they are initiating it? And who would make that decision? The family? The authorities? These are the sort of questions that Queen At Sea so admirably and desperately poses.

Really though, despite the inciting incident driving the film, it is ultimately about so much more than that: it is about the unfathomable quagmire of dementia. “I don’t know what’s going on in there anymore. She’s unreadable,” says Amanda at one point. Leslie – played so delicately and, to be honest, frighteningly by Calder-Marshall – seems in a state of constant confusion. When asked questions by authorities, her eyes plead to her daughter for help. The film is such a sympathetic portrayal of the loss of agency, of independence, of integrity and often dignity, and of the collateral damage on family members. Binoche’s Amanda is at her wit’s end, trying her best to navigate something not necessarily navigable, wanting the best for her mum and also for her own daughter, the teenage Sara (Florence Hunt), whose adolescence is being dramatically impinged by what’s happening.

The stakes are compounded by American writer/director Lance Hammer’s filmmaking which, for the early stretch at least, presents proceedings in a cold, matter-of-fact and brutal style, fixed cameras passively observing what’s happening. This creates a stark sense of unease, making the film feel intrusive and even voyeuristic, which is appropriate – this shouldn’t be comfortable. It’s a very effective approach from cinematographer Adolpho Veloso, who did such painterly work on last year’s Train Dreams .

There is an unflinching intimacy all round. A gynaecological examination. Amanda tenderly bathing her mother. The endless little heartbreaks. There’s not a line of dialogue that doesn’t seem like it’s being thought for the first time, let alone said, via unshowy, underplayed but incredibly powerful performances. Calder-Marshall is 79, Courtenay is 89; both are quietly but profoundly affecting. Meanwhile, the smaller, supporting characters – police, doctors, social workers and care-home staff – feel uncannily real. As it turns out, there’s a reason for that: in his efforts to make it all as accurate as possible, in terms of scenarios, terminology and even cadence, Hammer (who spent many years developing the film) consulted such staff and then asked them to appear on screen. The resulting authenticity makes for an even more confronting experience. (Also, if you know north London, Hammer captures Tufnell Park and Archway’s leafy and somewhat drab suburban tones so vividly – it’s shocking that it’s taken an American to get this right.)

Everything is so naturalistic and convincing that when events suddenly ratchet up at the end, it feels somewhat at odds with everything that’s come before – a bit of plot taking over from such a considered case study. A strand focusing on Amanda’s daughter Sara, meanwhile, also contrasts with the matter at hand, as she embarks on her own romantic pursuits. It’s a bittersweet reflection of where her grandmother finds herself, the world opening up for Sara, young love in full bloom, but feels like a nice conceit rather than a vital piece of the film. Still, among all the bleakness, its sweetness and warmth provide a welcome counterpoint, and a relief.

Humanity is key to Queen At Sea , which highlights some very knotty politics, illustrating that the system surrounding cases like Leslie’s can overwhelm and – despite the best wills in the world – dehumanise. For the most part, this film has a gentle touch, and you feel its despair throughout as it weighs it all up, posing difficult questions and not presuming to have any answers. It’s about the utter tragedy of dementia, about these poor people who have lost themselves, and the family members who have lost a substantial part of them. It’s a sad, sad film. You should see it.
review_summary: Appropriately and unavoidably bleak, and keenly understated, this is nevertheless a quietly enthralling piece of cinema, grappling with dementia both morally and mentally. Despairing, hugely compassionate work.

about_movie: Lowen (Dakota Johnson) is a struggling writer who is asked to help a bestselling author, Verity Crawford (Anne Hathaway), finish her crime novel. Verity’s husband Jeremy (Josh Hartnett) is supportive — but their house contains potentially deadly secrets…
review:
It takes a certain kind of mind to sit all day, imagining monstrous things, without becoming at least haunted by those dark visions — and perhaps consumed by them. At least, that's the premise of this thriller, adapted from a Colleen Hoover bestseller . But while struggling young crime writer Lowen (Dakota Johnson) is plagued by lots of suspicion and worried about possible manipulation, Verity never quite goes for the throat.

Johnson’s reserve suits Lowen, who's recently bereaved and further traumatised when she witnesses an accident right in front of her. Although she's yet to make her mark as an author, she hesitates to step into another woman's life and series when she's asked to help ghostwrite for best-selling crime writer Verity Crawford (Anne Hathaway), who has recently suffered both a death in the family and a devastating car crash. But she reconsiders after a personal plea from Crawford’s husband Jeremy, played by Josh Hartnett in full gee-shucks mode.

The first sign that she might have made a mistake is that Jeremy holds back just what kind of state Verity is in. Lowen reaches their (idyllic) house before she learns that the famous author is entirely catatonic and that she'll be working alone, from notes and fragments of ideas.

Naturally, it's not that simple. Lowen is haunted by the possibility that Verity is still, secretly, up and about, and distressed by the author's dark and twisted secret diary. But can she really trust Jeremy? Or her own perception? It’s all standard thriller stuff. Director Michael Showalter, who showed a sure hand with tone in the likes of The Big Sick , never quite feels as certain here; there's a lot of meandering around the beautiful modernist house and not much actual revelation, for all the occasionally creepy music cues and sudden cuts.

All three leads are on decent form: Hartnett likeable with just a hint of darkness underneath; Johnson unsettled but keeping it together; and Hathaway, largely seen in online clips and flashback, impossibly beautiful and eerily unreadable.

The issues here are more structural. The revelations of the last act are largely unscary and deeply unsatisfying, so that the film limps to a halt rather than building to a finale. Maybe it's trying to say something about looking too long and too deep into the abyss, but it mostly just mumbles about the importance of trust in relationships to no great effect instead.
review_summary: It's a solid enough melodrama elevated by overqualified leading ladies, but the twists and turns don't justify the lengthy running time.

about_movie: When new-in-town teenager Naim (Joe Bird) starts a relationship with his classmate, Ryan (Stacy Clausen), his mother (Mia Wasikowska) and her local church employ a deliverance healer (Nicholas Hope) to “cure” their urges. But the cure soon turns out to be a curse.
review:
With its enigmatic Biblical title, and acknowledged debt to It Follows , Australian writer-director Adrian Chiarella’s debut horror may sound derivative. Yet the fears bubbling beneath the surface are so vivid, it easily transcends its inspirations.

Naim (Joe Bird), love interest Ryan (Stacy Clausen) and Hunter (Jeremy Blewitt), who Ryan also messes around with, are ordinary kids trying to understand their sexualities. But because of the god-fearing backwater they live in, they are forbidden from being themselves. Chiarella grew up in Sydney, but he has a feel for the textures and strictures of rural town life: the empty arcades and derelict factories; the sense that there is nothing to do but have sex, fight or leave.

Leviticus refers to the Bible chapter that forbids homosexuality, or so conservative Christians believe, and the ritual Naim, Ryan and Hunter are forced to undergo is horrifying — almost as bad as Bird’s gruesome fate in Talk To Me . Instead of finding themselves saved, however, they are instead stalked by demons who take the form of their loved ones, attacking them at school, at work, anywhere they are alone. The debt to It Follows here is so strong it may as well be a sequel . But it’s one David Robert Mitchell could be proud of.

With the help of a gorgeous score and luminous cinematography, Chiarella captures the flare of first love, alongside some memorable scares. A sequence in which Naim, home alone, has to defend himself against an interloper escalates from fight-or-flight panic to shocking violence in a moment.

At times the subtext — that, for LGBTQ+ people, openly loving someone can be the greatest danger — is stretched almost to breaking point. But Chiarella never allows us to forget that the fight is real, and as scary as anything the movies could make up. What emerges is precious indeed: a fright flick that has something to say, and lots of ugly/beautiful ways to say it.
review_summary: Chiarella’s heartfelt horror is a tender coming-of-age drama spiked with terrifying home truths.

about_movie: Two police officers (Hwang Jung-min and Hoyeon) in a small town near the demilitarised zone between North and South Korea find themselves under attack from a mysterious creature unlike anything they’ve seen before.
review:
Given that Hope has made headlines as South Korea’s most expensive movie of all time, you might expect that director Na Hong-jin’s latest would play it safe and deliver a more traditional blockbuster. Yet in its opening moments, as a police chief follows a path of destruction left by a mysterious creature across his small DMZ town, this Spielbergian monster-mystery soon reveals itself to be a far bigger (and more insane) swing than the likes of Super 8 or Cloverfield , where monsters simply run wild. This is a very different beast — and by far the most gonzo film of the year.

Hope is a hard film to put in a box. It’s an insane two-and-a-half-hour monster movie with a brutal ‘how-the-hell-did-they-film-that?’ foot-to-horse-to-car extended chase, a serious lengthy monologue about diarrhoea (which is a crucial plot point), and, to top it all off, Michael Fassbender and Alicia Vikander rock up at one point and make jaw-to-the-floor appearances. These bizarre tonal switches just shouldn’t work, yet its embrace of mayhem on screen marks it as one of the year’s most entertaining cinema experiences.

Not since Mad Max: Fury Road has a film slammed its foot down on the accelerator so hard. Even when holding its cards to its chest and not revealing the creature itself, the film goes full steam ahead, keeping us hot on its path of destruction. A tense first hour makes way for some of the silliest (and most impressive) action of the year as the cat-and-mouse game gets flipped on its head. Yet for all the film’s entertainment value, the one caveat is that you will have to get past its less-than-perfect CGI.

Amid the madness, though, there is also depth. The town of Hope Harbour, in proximity to North Korea and riddled with signs about not trusting strangers, immediately goes on the attack when something otherworldly breaches its walls. Those looking for something beyond explosions will find plenty to love here as the film unpicks a small community deeply set in its ways.

With buildings being destroyed and guns firing every few seconds, Hope isn’t a film concerned with going too deep on its characters. It’s to the film’s benefit, then, that its two leads, Hwang Jung-min and Hoyeon, are such a presence on screen. Hwang’s initial gruff exterior soon makes way to reveal an officer floundering and in way over his head. But it is Hoyeon, who enters the film firing off a grenade-launcher, who cements herself as an action star here, balancing the film’s more tender moments while being equally convincing firing off thousands of rifle rounds.

A lore-heavy final ten minutes makes clear this is only Part 1, and may leave some viewers questioning what on earth they just saw — the film’s vigour somewhat diluted after nearly three hours of adrenaline with no a final pay-off. But those won over by another insane vision from one of Korea’s most impressive filmmakers will be left kicking and screaming for more.
review_summary: Do yourself a favour and surrender to this entertaining, unwieldy and goofy spectacle. Much like its monster, it runs amok. Bring on Part 2!

movie_name_try2: Oasis: Don’t Look Back In Anger Review
about_movie: The long-awaited reunion of Liam and Noel Gallagher, and Oasis’ historic Live ’25 world tour, is captured on film as it happened.
review:
“When Oasis split up, everything went to shit.” So asserts a typically erudite Liam Gallagher in Don’t Look Back In Anger over shots of Donald Trump, Elon Musk, Theresa May, and other lowlights of the years since he and brother Noel’s acrimonious 2009 split. Did the break-up of a Britpop band actually break the world? Of course not. But did their return last summer — tambourines, bucket hats, elongated vowels and all — start to make it better? Documentarians Dylan Southern and Will Lovelace, alongside writer Steven Knight ( Peaky Blinders ), certainly think so. And they make a hell of a case here.

There’s been no shortage of blockbuster concert movies in recent years. The likes of Taylor Swift, Billie Eilish and Beyoncé’s recorded tours have all thrived in a landscape where the communal escape live music provides has breached monopolistic ticket sellers’ containment. What sets Don’t Look Back In Anger apart is the way it so lovingly, holistically captures the Live ’25 phenomenon as it happened. It’s a mercurial blend of introspective rock-doc and immersive concert experience boasting near- Get Back levels of “I can’t believe this footage exists” moments. (Liam’s first rehearsal arrival feels, in several senses, biblical.)

From early-doors rehearsal-room reconciliation to final-night ‘Champagne Supernova’ stadium singalongs via pun-stuffed police briefings, sledgehammer-subtle sermons on forgiveness (a rare, over-scripted misstep), and a slew of memorable encounters with passionate mad-fer-its from Burnage to Brazil, Don’t Look Back In Anger indelibly crystallises a moment when doing the Poznań and belting out ‘Cigarettes & Alcohol’ with fans of all ages, nations, and backgrounds genuinely felt like the answer to modern society’s collective malaise. That the cinematographer likes of The Brutalist ’s Lol Crawley and Moonlight ’s James Laxton are behind the cameras, reverently framing moments of chaos and cathartic release in emotionally charged close-ups and awe-inspiring wide shots, certainly doesn’t hurt.

As anyone who’s seen Lovelace and Southern’s past films about LCD Soundsystem , Blur , and New York’s turn-of-the-millennium indie scene will be well aware, the doc-making duo have a gift for taking cinematic snapshots of a cultural landscape and, within that, intimate portraits of their subjects. And while occasionally the scope of the duo’s work can compromise its depth (Noel and Liam’s much-hyped first joint interview in decades, while a sweary delight, could have absolutely used more of the time elsewhere spent labouring a deep-sea-diving metaphor in South Korea), this is such a rollicking paean to the unifying power of music that — in the spirit of the Gallaghers themselves — any minor foibles will be forgiven.
review_summary: An epic summer for Oasis fans becomes a euphoric cinematic experience. It’s not perfect, but it’s definitely, maybe the decade’s best concert movie yet.

about_movie: Soviet Russia, 1987. US Navy pilot Troy Kelly (Ryan Reynolds) crashes behind enemy lines during a Black Ops mission, and his only chance at getting home is teaming up with ex-KGB agent and Top Gun mega-fan Nikolai (Kenneth Branagh).
review:
When you hear the words “buddy-comedy action movie starring Ryan Reynolds”, you probably feel like you have a good idea of what to expect — some slick fights, endless witty quips, and a reasonably entertaining time. Mayday delivers on all of that, and a little bit more.

The film opens with Reynolds’ pilot, Troy, waking up post-crash-landing, a huge bit of plane poking out of his leg and an unknown potential adversary walking towards him, right as he passes out. It’s a very Deadpool -esque, record-scratch, ‘you’re probably wondering how I got here’ moment, but Mayday never fully succumbs to Reynolds’ most grating one-liner-spouting tendencies. It instead balances his comedic charm with genuine tenderness — Troy is just a guy who loves flying planes, loves his dad, and (as he learns in quite a clichéd way, misguidedly) loves his country.

Turns out that potential adversary was in fact a newfound friend, in the form of Kenneth Branagh’s straight-talking, slightly unsettling Nikolai Ustinov. Obsessed with an idealistic version of the USA, his bootleg copy of Top Gun and the promise of tasting a McDonald’s, Nikolai’s also a lethal ex-KGB agent, and gets almost all of the cool action moments in this movie — think hand-to-hand combat, a police chase involving a nuclear missile, and enough pool-fu to make John Wick jealous.

Game Night and Dungeons & Dragons: Honour Among Thieves directing duo John Francis Daley and Jonathan Goldstein bring their signature filmmaking flair to said action moments, swinging their camera around, attaching it to car doors and dropping in impactful overhead angles — a lovely side-shot of Nikolai and Troy driving their car against numerous rural and urban Russian backdrops sticks in the mind. The sequence of Troy’s plane crash is also impressive, with one shot tracking him flipping the plane vertically, ejecting right before the enemy aircraft hits, and perilously parachuting down to the ground.

This camera trickery is vital in elevating _Mayda_y’s thoroughly conventional script, and while Maria Bakalova brings a lot of heart with barely any screen time as Nikolai’s estranged daughter Anna, Reynolds and Branagh’s crackling odd-couple chemistry is the star of the show. Throw in some almost interesting gestures towards questioning American patriotism, and the morality of a nation that consistently casts itself as the hero, and you’ve got a genuinely entertaining, if highly predictable, watch.
review_summary: No need to declare an emergency here — thanks to two compelling central performances from Ryan Reynolds and Kenneth Branagh, engaging aesthetics and well-choreographed fight scenes, Mayday makes for a solid comedy-action combo.

about_movie: Four childhood friends who never hang out decide to escape the drudgery of their daily lives by going to a spa resort. But one friend, Mel (Isla Fisher), is desperate to have a wilder weekend than they expected. Chaos ensues.
review:
Filmmaking team Jon Lucas and Scott Moore made their name by writing the original screenplay for 2009’s The Hangover , in which three friends and their weird mate get blackout drunk on a stag do. That film was the archetype, the bedrock text, the Dead Sea Scroll of early 2000s-2010s ‘kerrazzzy party’ movies. Since then, Lucas and Moore have made a career out of leaning into this mould, producing variations on that raunchily hedonistic theme: from 21 & Over (three friends get blackout drunk on a 21st birthday) to Bad Moms (three mothers get blackout drunk because they’re stressed) and A Bad Moms Christmas (three mothers get blackout drunk, but at Christmas).

Spa Weekend is the latest innovation on that highly original template. The set-up for this alleged comedy is as perfunctory as they come: three childhood friends in their forties — lawyer and single mum Jane (Leslie Mann), hard-working Sophie (Anna Faris), and hothead divorcee Coco (Michelle Buteau) — lament the fact that they never hang out anymore. On a whim, they book a spa weekend at a luxury resort, owned by a woman with a mystifying English-ish accent. By accident, they also invite their estranged pal, Aussie wildcard Mel (Isla Fisher), who sends the weekend into catastrophic chaos.

It’s hard to know what’s more offensive about this film. For one thing, it boasts among the most reductive ideas possible of what it thinks women want: male strippers, mud baths, meditation, and dry humping. The hunky love interest, Adam Demos’ yoga instructor Kai, seems like a 1990s conception of what straight women want out of a man, with his cheese-grater abs and slow-motion blond tips; even Peter Andre would think it was old-fashioned.

Far more unpleasant is the presence of Isla Fisher’s Mel, who falls into the Zach-Galifianakis-in- The-Hangover mould, the weirdo outsider who the others can’t stand. But where Galifianakis’ Alan was at least charmingly clueless, Mel is genuinely hateful, an obnoxious presence with an almost Trumpian lack of self-awareness, whose only purpose is destruction and harm. The antics she gets up to — she joyrides a golf buggy! She lets goats loose on the resort! She is loud in a meditation class! — are hopelessly contrived and unfunny, amounting to genuinely toxic behaviour, which is summarily forgiven by her pals.

The cast are all talented comedic actors who at least find pockets of charisma amid the terribly written script, and having an all-female cast in a theatrically released major studio comedy is no small feat. Women should be allowed to be just as disgusting and obnoxious as men in our comedies. But maybe let’s get someone other than these two blokes writing and directing it next time.
review_summary: This Hangover facsimile — ‘Eat, Pray, Shag’, if you like — is an insult to the female audience it is targeting. Even the hen do crowds will be unimpressed.

movie_name: Original Title:The Death Of Robin Hood
movie_name_try2: The Death Of Robin Hood Review
about_movie: Nearing the end of his life, legendary outlaw Robin Hood (Jackman) travels to a monastery, where his past finally catches up with him.
review:
There are no Merry Men in The Death Of Robin Hood . In fact, it’s pretty low on merriment all round. Based on a 17th-century ballad, this bleak and brutal drama takes a blood-soaked battle axe to one of Britain’s most enduring legends, of a courageous bandit who robbed from the rich to give to the poor. What if that icon were in fact a monster, the film asks? Someone who slaughtered and stole for pleasure? A man confused and quietly tortured by how tales of his violent exploits had somehow entered folklore? In its opening 30 minutes, children are slain and eyes are gouged before this version of the noble archer impales a person’s face with a flaming spike. A bushy-tailed cartoon fox or man in tights , this Robin Hood most certainly is not.

The film stars Hugh Jackman back in Logan terrain, playing another grizzled warrior worn down after a life of violence. Like Wolverine in that 2017 super-coda, his Hood is thrust into caring for a young girl, who awakens in him a new appreciation for life. After suffering gruesome injuries in a late-night attack on the farm his best friend Little John (Bill Skarsgård) calls home, Hood is taken to a remote island, where Jodie Comer’s Sister Brigid attempts to heal him. There, he develops a connection with Margaret (Faith Delaney) — Little John’s daughter — that opens his soul to all the things he missed out on amid his senseless campaigns of carnage.

Writer-director Michael Sarnoski has made a name for himself with stories about complicated loners like this, who cling to a single source of joy. In 2021’s Pig , it was a prized swine; in 2024 alien-invasion prequel A Quiet Place: Day One , it was a New York pizzeria. In The Death Of Robin Hood , it’s the found-family that Hood discovers in this gentle hideaway that gives him reason to stay alive. In Margaret, Brigid and a nameless leper wrapped head-to-toe in cloth, played by The White Lotus ’ Murray Bartlett, he begins to learn, for the first time, to put down his bow.

Like with his previous films, Sarnoski coaxes brilliantly tender performances from his cast, and captures rural splendour like few other directors operating right now. After a punishing first act, shot in sombre greys, the movie erupts into colour as Jackman’s wounded killer contemplates his past. For some, what follows might feel like an unsatisfying left-turn. A plot thread involving Noah Jupe ( Hamnet ) as Arthur, a new arrival at the monastery, teases a bloody comeuppance that never arrives. Instead, Sarnoski condemns Hood to a final showdown with a foe far more menacing than any mace-waving maniac — his own crumbling conscience.
review_summary: Beautifully understated after its initial bombast, this won’t be for everyone. For those with patience, however, it’s a poignant meditation on myth and the futility of violence.
