about_movie: Ex-soldier James (Brad Pitt) and his dog Odin (Uber) are camping in the Alaskan mountains when a storm cuts their trip short. James suffers a heart attack while flying his plane home, stranding the pair in the wilderness.
review:
In the opening scene of Heart Of The Beast , director David Ayer assures the audience the dog will survive everything we’re about to watch. He literally shows us he’s fine… and then spends the better part of 100 minutes making us stressfully wonder if he was somehow, unforgivably, lying.

The film begins with a van approaching Odin (Uber), a German Shepherd standing alone in the middle of a remote road. As the driver goes to greet him, we flash back to a week earlier. Odin is sitting in a plane’s cockpit beside his owner, James (Brad Pitt), who’s flying them to a camping trip in the Alaskan mountains. Evidently, James and Odin do this a lot and are well trained for it. James is a retired US Army Special Forces officer and Odin his also-retired military working dog. James left service with some scars and a yearning for solitude. Odin left with one prosthetic leg and PTSD-induced nightmares. These two are best friends. When James has a heart attack while trying to fly home, they crash land and are stuck in the middle of nowhere, entirely reliant on each other for survival.

From that set-up, Heart Of The Beast takes a largely predictable path, with James and Odin saving each other from roaring rivers, wild animals and various falls, but that’s not a negative. It hits the expected beats satisfyingly and with earned emotion. Ayer, a director whose CV is packed with testosteroney films like End Of Watch , the Pitt-starring Fury and several Jason Statham joints, is more than capable of putting together a solid action-adventure, but here he also knows when to get mushy. Through the many thrilling, very well-paced action sequences he keeps establishing James and Odin’s connection. The script, by Cameron Alexander, divvies up the heroism — for instance, Odin tries to revive James as his heart attack hits; James nurses Odin after the crash, so it’s not just about a very loyal dog. It’s a mutual, very sweet protection.

Aside from two brief supporting roles, one from J.K. Simmons as another adventurer/expository device, this is effectively a two-hander. Or one-hand, one-pawer. It rests on an authentic bond between man and dog. Pitt creates a convincing relationship while effectively talking to himself, and Uber is edited excellently to suggest doggy-thinking. Ayer only very occasionally over-anthropomorphises the dog ­— that canine nightmare sequence is a bit daft. Mostly, he plays it just cute enough. He makes you root for both to make it and, even though he’s already shown us how it ends, keeps the tension high enough that you still fret about what might happen. If you are a dog-lover, bring tissues. If you are a dog-owner, bring a friend to help you get home.
review_summary: You couldn’t want much more from a one-man-and-his-dog survival tale. A very good movie about a very good boy.

about_movie: A courier (Austin Abrams) takes a high-priority late-night delivery into Raccoon City — only to discover that a series of mutated humans stand between him and his destination.
review:
“Itchy. Tasty.” These are the iconic last words of a man succumbing to the deadly T-Virus in 1996’s original Resident Evil video game. That is the central conceit of the horror series: a virus that rewrites DNA, stripping its infected of humanity, turning them into horrifying flesh-craving creatures. Yet across seven critically panned film adaptations, the simple premise of the games — bumbling your way through a sticky situation with limited bullets while facing hordes of infected — is yet to be authentically captured on film. Enter actor-turned-horror-filmmaker Zach Cregger, whose take attempts to wipe the slate clean. Gone is the earlier film franchise ’s Milla Jovovich’s Alice, the game series’ Leon Kennedy or any prior convoluted lore. Instead, this lands as one of the most video game-y video-game adaptations to ever grace our screens — for better and for worse.

As a director, Cregger is first and foremost an entertainer. His first two films, Barbarian and Weapons , with their Rubik’s Cube structures and shifting perspectives, are impeccably made theme-park rides. Resident Evil represents Cregger in his most no-frills form: an A-to-B, man-on-a-mission movie that doesn’t lean into his box of narrative tricks. This is his midnight movie, stripping things back to setpiece after setpiece, less focused on logic and more on spilling bodily fluids. While there’s no doubt that exploding bodies and pulsating blood bags are going to be a near-perfect pairing with a packed-out cinema and a side of popcorn on a Friday night, some of Cregger’s flourishes are missed.

It’s on an icy road on the outskirts of Raccoon City where Resident Evil really gets its hooks — or tendrils — into you. A persistent uneasiness takes hold as things go from bad to worse. What starts as an accidental roadside encounter swiftly turns into a playful series of terrors. Cregger hits every horror beat he can muster, with some masterful misdirects and scares, foregrounding everything from the creak of a floorboard to the number of bullets left in a gun chamber. It’s rare that a film’s first act so confidently engulfs you in someone’s point of view, with its leering camera, POV shots and outright refusal to lean on cheap scares. When the jolts do come, they hit hard.

Just as Raccoon City swallows up Austin Abrams’ unfortunate courier Bryan, the film begins to somewhat lose its footing. Its second act lacks real direction, leaning heavily into horror-comedy — weighted more to the comedy — while getting a little too meta for its own good. Cregger does such a good job of translating the game’s DNA into movie form — from gun upgrades to Bryan’s growing confidence playing out like a literal video game-esque skill tree — that it’s a shame when the film starts spelling out the joke. When he shouts, “I’m only good at guns in games,” the first of many self-aware smirks, it actively draws too much attention to its gaming roots, when the film was doing so well embracing them. Thankfully the film finds its footing, and a clearer direction, in a final act, which embraces its source material’s campy roots.

The glue holding this all together is Austin Abrams. In him, Cregger has found the bumbling, chaotic De Niro to his Scorsese. Playing Bryan as an even bigger goofball here than his scuzzy character in Weapons , this hapless everyman is the ideal punching bag to the horrors that ensue. Abrams performs it perfectly, knowing exactly how to look hopeless holding a shotgun, traumatised when covered in blood, and hit comedy beats as if improvised.

Which all makes sense for a series like this. Resident Evil as both a video game and film franchise has never left us much substantial to chew on, thematically. The video game’s most iconic moments range from a man punching a boulder, to memorably cheesy dialogue ("That was too close... you were almost a Jill sandwich!"). So it’s not much of a surprise that, as the credits roll, there’s not much to reflect on, save for 90 thoroughly entertaining minutes. Sinking into your seat, scared one moment and giggling the next, is the Resident Evil experience the games have always offered, and the one Cregger has finally managed to capture. Itchy. Tasty. Bloody. Sticky. And all the rest.
review_summary: More than clears the (fairly low) bar as the best Resident Evil movie yet. While its rollicking first act matches the promise of Weapons or Barbarian, its surprise-free narrative stops it short of ascending those heights. But horror fans will happily gobble up this tight, bloody, 90-minute thrill-ride.

movie_name: Original Title:Shaun The Sheep: The Beast Of Mossy Bottom
movie_name_try2: Shaun The Sheep: The Beast Of Mossy Bottom Review
about_movie: When the clumsy Farmer (John Sparkes) ruins the pumpkin patch, Shaun (Justin Fletcher) experiments to rescue the crop — accidentally creating a monster.
review:
Who or what is Britain’s greatest cultural export? Is it James Bond? Doctor Who ? MoneySavingExpert’s Martin Lewis? There is an extremely strong case to be made that it is, in fact, Shaun The Sheep, the claymation lamb with a heart of gold, whose silent-movie-esque antics, dialogue-free save for bleats and grunts, have made him a hero in over 170 countries, his family-friendly slapstick humour crossing borders worldwide.

So it goes with this, the third Shaun big-screen outing, a continuation of a media empire that began with a supporting role in the 1995 Wallace and Gromit short A Close Shave and has since spawned films, TV shows, spin-offs, and a very lucrative line of merchandise (Shaun The Sheep-branded body spray, yours for just £34.99). Where the first film was the franchise’s take on Babe: Pig In The City , and the second, 2019’s Farmageddon , a cute alien-invasion sci-fi pastiche, The Beast Of Mossy Bottom leans more into the horror side, as Aardman Animation, with its love of old-school B-movies (see also: Wallace & Gromit: The Curse Of The Were-Rabbit ), is wont to do.

Think Frankenstein crossed with The Wolf Man , only with Plasticine farmyard animals, and you’re not far off. Here, Shaun (voiced, as ever, by Mr Tumble himself, Justin Fletcher) and his loyal flock are Halloween-obsessed and desperate to make Jack O’Lanterns worthy of the season. When a freak accident knocks out their crop of prize pumpkins, Shaun turns to mad science — aptly adopting a mad scientist get-up in the process — and, via a hilarious turn of events, accidentally transforms his beloved if ungainly Farmer (John Sparkes) into a Bigfoot-like monster who terrorises the local village.

It’s a classic lark. The commitment to silliness is genuinely admirable, and while this is defiantly precision-engineered for young children, as all Shaun outings are — the now-standard pop-music montage will have kids dancing in the aisles — there is plenty for adults to lap up. Expect just as many jokes that might fly over children’s heads (spot the sly references to Hitchcock and Hammer) as there are all-ages gags (pigs playing Jenga is funny, however old you are).

What is most impressive, though, is how Aardman’s stop-motion care and craft remains as sharp as ever. This is directed by Steve Cox and Matthew Walker in their feature debuts, but feels as warm and witty as any Wallace & Gromit or Chicken Run . For 50 years now, Aardman has been making animated magic from the suburbs of Bristol, and its most lovable mascot confirms the studio is still in rude health.
review_summary: Daft and delightful, as all Shaun The Sheep escapades are. This is what properly good kids’ entertainment looks like.

about_movie: The friendship of boarding-school students Minna (Galaxie Clear) and Flic (Marni Duggan) is dramatically tested when they embark on a summer project to fall in love.
review:
The Charli XCX lyric, “It’s so confusing sometimes to be a girl,” is a perfect descriptor for the core ethos of Molly Manners’ charmingly offbeat directorial debut. Focusing on the graduation from girlhood to womanhood, Extra Geography joins the growing canon of British films that take teenage girlhood seriously, like Rocks and Last Swim , but Manners’ film offers a fresh take on friends growing  up and apart.

Based on Rose Tremain’s 2007 short story, Succession writer Miriam Battye opens the film with confident Minna (Galaxie Clear) and timid Flic (Marni Duggan) lying on the lacrosse field worrying about their future and Oxbridge applications. With no boys, drugs or part-time jobs to distract them from their studies, their main concern is to become more “worldly” with a simple summer project: to fall in love. The subject of their experiment turns out to be their flustered geography teacher, Miss Delavigne (Alice Englert).

However, this endeavour divides the girls for the first time. A production of A Midsummer Night’s Dream steals Minna’s focus: she’s Fairy Queen Titania and hangs out with boys from a neighbouring school, while Flic is cast as a tree, and so she dives into studying love as an academic pursuit. Jealousy wedges itself between them and their friendship starts to wilt. Mirroring the Shakespeare play, Extra Geography takes on a five-act structure, but the film’s balancing act of several narrative threads unfortunately becomes tangled as its razor-sharp bite isn’t sustained across the full 94 minutes.

While Manners and Battye deserve credit for their deft handling of teen angst with brooding desires and snappy comedic one-liners, the commanding performances of Clear and Duggan are the real triumph here. This formative, symbiotic friendship is beautifully lived-in, with the fresh-faced actors capturing the ugly, strange and impulsive reality of teenage girlhood.

This oddly endearing coming-of-age drama is contained to the isolated boarding school, which serves as a well-lit dollhouse for them to roam, suspended in time and place. Though this creates some beguilling visuals, the film’s handling of class (Minna holidaying in Lanzarote while Flic is reminded she’s on a scholarship) and emerging queer sexuality (hints at sapphic longing permeate dreamy frames) raises interesting ideas but falls short at grappling with the nuances of it all. What prevails, though, is an original and painfully accurate portrait of first love being your best friend.
review_summary: A confident debut. Though some areas are lightly sketched, the riveting performances from two promising newcomers are deserving of a pass with merit.

about_movie: Biotech professor Kwon Se-jeong (Jun Ji-hyun) and a small group of survivors fight to stay alive during a zombie outbreak. But the infected are evolving, and their only hope for a cure lies with Seo Young-cheol (Koo Kyo-hwan), the twisted genius who created this virus in the first place.
review:
You’d be forgiven for assuming Korean filmmaker Yeon Sang-ho might be done with zombies. After he injected fresh blood into the genre with Train To Busan , the momentum continued with his animated prequel, Seoul Station , but was stopped in its tracks by Peninsula , Yeon’s poorly received sequel. Yet zombies are notoriously hard to put down, even for masters of the genre, it turns out, because Yeon is back at it again with a new undead thriller titled Colony .

Well, in fact these zombies aren’t undead. Not exactly. While previous efforts were less concerned with outbreak mechanics, Colony stands out precisely because of its unique approach to the ways in which these zombies operate. Never mind slow or fast or whatever else you’ve seen before — the zombies born of this specifically engineered virus are connected through a hive-mind, using their collective intelligence to adapt against whatever the humans throw their way. Watching them writhe and spasmodically seize in unison as they communicate is chilling — even more so than what comes next. That too remains horrifying, as the infected trip over themselves trying to reach their victims, running and flipping and crawling with a gruesome ferocity brought to life through the use of dancers and contortionists.

And what of those victims? Scientist Kwon Se-jeong (Jun Ji-hyun) and her motley band of survivors are easy to root for, if a tad underdeveloped. The architect of the virus, Seo Young-cheol (Koo Kyo-hwan), is far more interesting, providing a human face to the evils that unfold. Peninsula 's Koo plays a different role here, bringing his zombie leader to life with a detached, psychotic swagger that might actually have you considering his argument, that these zombies are an upgrade on what humanity has to offer. That the film itself doesn't delve into this more isn't so much of a drawback as it is a byproduct of the intense focus on survival, more concerned with running and flipping and crawling to the next set-piece with a near-cartoonish bloodlust and frenzy.
review_summary: While not as evolved as the zombies themselves, Colony darts around and develops classic tropes, further establishing Yeon as the George A. Romero of today.

about_movie: A bunch of tourists looking for alligators on a Louisiana bayou come under attack from a hungry, hungry hippo.
review:
Hippotamuses in pop culture have mostly been treated warmly. From the dancing kind in Disney’s Fantasia to Jada Pinkett Smith’s Gloria in Madagascar to George in ITV kids’ staple Rainbow , the semi-aquatic mammals have often been presented as gentle, benign and surprisingly nimble. Writer-director James Nunn’s Hungry — the title itself riffs on the fun, frantic table-top game Hungry Hungry Hippos — tries to redress the balance by turning Hippopotamus amphibius into an unstoppable killing machine, a mud-bound Anton Chigurh without the bad hair. Unfortunately, this homicidal hippo is pretty much the only thing Hungry has going for it.

The hackneyed premise throws together a band of thinly drawn holidaymakers who take a boat trip around the bayou to see some ’gators run by hunky captain Rodrigo (Michel Curiel). So, we have retired fireman-with-a-dead-wife Tim (Jim Meskimen), his uptight middle-aged daughter Sally (Samantha Coughlan) and Sally’s stroppy/horny teenage son Mike (River Codack) plus business-type Dionne (Tracey Bonner), who is estranged from her step-kids and insists on wearing stilettos in swamp country.

Livening up the proceedings are party girl Hannah (Olivia Bernstone) and most importantly of all, her bestie Sistine (Madison Davenport), a self-described failure who has just been fired from her minimum wage job and is struggling to care for her sick mother. From the get-go, it is clear that Sistine has big Final Girl energy, partly because she is nice, partly because she is resourceful and partly because she is named after a chapel.

Because historically hippos don’t pose much of a threat, Nunn’s script works hard to establish their menacing bona fides. Enter Walker (Joaquim de Almeida), a kind of Quint of hippos who tells everyone the animal may be vegetarian but weighs 3.5 tons, is responsible for 500 human deaths a year and “kills for fun”.

After the hippo upturns the tour boat, the film is mostly set in a tree as the characters struggle to stay out of the water and come up with bone-headed plans for escape. The hippo is mostly represented by water-level POV shots but when he turns up on screen, he is an effective, enjoyably practical predator. He frankly gives a more nuanced performance than anyone else.

There is probably a fun movie in killer hippos — it’s just a shame Hungry has little sense of its own ridiculousness. None of the kills delight. It comes to something when the scariest thing about the film is the NOW TV thumbnail.
review_summary: Starring a fun prosthetic creature, Hungry is not here for a long time or a good time. Hippos, you had your chance and you blew it. Bring on the violent vole movies.

movie_name: Original Title:Gail Daughtry And The Celebrity Sex Pass
movie_name_try2: Gail Daughtry And The Celebrity Sex Pass Review
about_movie: When her fiancé uses his celebrity sex pass — the idea that you can sleep with one celebrity without repercussions — Kansas hairdresser Gail Daughtry (Zoey Deutch) heads to Los Angeles and embarks on a wild journey to level the score by sleeping with hers: Jon Hamm (Jon Hamm).
review:
Don’t do it. Don’t be that person. Don’t be that person who turns their nose up at the prospect of seeing Gail Daughtry And The Celebrity Sex Pass , doubtless put off by either that unwieldy title (who the hell is Gail Daughtry? What the actual eff is a celebrity sex pass?) or its knock-down-ginger release strategy, finally appearing on UK cinema screens two months after its opening in America, but with zero promotion or publicity, more a rumour than a release.

Because if you are that person, you’ll be missing out. Missing out on some serious bragging rights when, ten years from now, Gail Daughtry And The Celebrity Sex Pass begins appearing on Letterboxd lists like The Greatest Comedies Of The 21st Century or hectoring think-pieces entitled something like The Best Comedies You’ve Never Seen (And Why You Should Feel Ashamed That You Haven’t Seen Them). Because if you are not that person, you’ll be able to don a smug grin and say, “I was there. I was there right at the beginning for Gail Daughtry And The Celebrity Sex Pass . And yes, that title still sucks.”

Because Gail Daughtry And The Celebrity Sex Pass is arguably the funniest film of the year (so far; there’s still a chance it could be eclipsed by Paul Greengrass’ The Uprising ), with writer-director David Wain and writer-star Ken Marino deliberately, determinedly throwing every joke they could think of into the mix, along with virtually every style of comedy that exists. Sight gags, puns, surrealist humour, OTT violence, meta nods and winks — it’s all here. And while not everything hits, the hit-rate is astonishing, and while this isn’t a direct parody, the gag-rate recalls the halcyon days of Zucker-Abrahams-Zucker and Mel Brooks.

It is, though, an utterly demented riff on The Wizard Of Oz , with the innocent hairdresser Gail Daughtry (or Dorothy Gale) and her best friend Otto (have a wild guess what that’s an anagram of) going from Kansas to a land even more demented than Oz: Los Angeles. There, they team up with three utter buffoons in need of a heart, a brain, and courage (Ben Wang, Marino, and John Slattery, on extraordinary form as a total nitwit called John Slattery), who band together to help Gail achieve her goal: to get revenge on her feckless fiancé, who used his Celebrity Sex Pass to cheat on Gail with the A-list Jennifer Aniston, by slammin’ ham with Jon Hamm.

However, unbeknownst to Gail and the gang, a wicked witch of the West Coast, Sabrina Impacciatore’s Mafia boss Ludovica, wants Gail dead, for reasons, and has dispatched her best/worst henchmen (Joe Lo Truglio and Mather Zickel) to track her down.

Will Gail find the yellow brick road that leads to the Hamm behind the curtain? And what will happen behind said curtain if she does meet him? Who will survive, and what will be left of them? The fun is in finding out, as Wain and Marino stud Gail’s path with deliciously daft moments (an extended Slattery/door interface is arguably the film’s funniest bit) and ridiculous obstacles, all of which she meets with boundless enthusiasm. The cast, often bolstered by cameos pulled straight from Wain’s big black book of comedy all-stars (including Wain himself), is outstanding, but it’s the extraordinary Zoey Deutch who is the magic glue, able to effortlessly navigate the film’s frequent tonal shifts with aplomb.

Deutch, who, as the daughter of Pretty In Pink director Howard Deutch and Back To The Future ’s Lea Thompson, seemed almost genetically engineered to be a light comedian, has been superb for a few years now, in the likes of Zombieland: Double Tap , Richard Linklater’s Nouvelle Vague , and Voicemails For Isabelle . But this is her biggest role yet, and she snatches the opportunity with both hands, able to smoothly sell those tonal shifts even as Gail’s journey takes her from a naive urchin who thinks tipping 79 cents is generous to… well, that would be spoiling things. But let’s just say there are things that sweet, innocent Gail does that only an actor of considerable charm could pull off. It’s the kind of role that could launch her as a major comedy star, if more than four people see it. Let’s hope that happens.

In a way, it’s apt that this movie comes out in 2026, 25 years after Wain and Marino launched their careers (and about a dozen others, many of whom show up here) with Wet Hot American Summer , a movie that died upon release and now shows up frequently on those Letterboxd lists and think-pieces. That seems almost certain to be Gail Daughtry And The Celebrity Sex Pass ’ fate, but it doesn’t have to be that way. You can do something about it. So get out there and do it. Be on the right side of history. Spread the word. But maybe, when you’re spreading the word, just call the film ‘Gail Daughtry’. It’ll be easier that way.
review_summary: A constant joy from director David Wain, with gags of all kinds, shapes and sizes vying for your attention, and what should be a star-making performance from Zoey Deutch. Don’t pass on it because of the title.

about_movie: 1933. Offered a lifeline by Warden Clancy (Russell Crowe), ex-convict Samuel Murphy (Ethan Hawke) agrees to smuggle gold across Oregon, but his freedom comes at a cost.
review:
A breakout at this year’s Sundance, Padraic McKinley’s grimly determined debut is an indie throwback to the man-versus-wild movies of the ’70s: gritty films like the Robert Redford-starrer Jeremiah Johnson , or The Last Hard Men . Admittedly, The Weight ’s impact is lighter than the title suggests, and sticks to formula like a superglued barnacle, but here’s another showcase for the endlessly versatile Ethan Hawke: truly the Swiss Army knife of acting.

We meet his car mechanic Murphy hurtling towards skid row: jobless, homeless, and after a scuffle with cops, sentenced to a labour camp. “When I get out,” he tells his daughter Penny. “I’m gonna come get you.”  That promise is the fuel to Murphy’s dying fire. Four months later, he’s cracking rocks with a chain gang and building a road to nowhere. A tenuous bond with Russell Crowe’s warden leads to an offer he can’t refuse. The government are seizing gold. Black Hawk Mine is next. Lead a crew through 50 miles of wilderness, deliver the bullion at a rendezvous and he’s a free man. Cue a men-on-a-mission movie in Depression-era rags.

The Weight gropes for a consistent tone in its overlong first act, finally finding its pulse in the savage wilds of Oregon. As Murphy’s band of felons grapple with the wilderness (and each other), those looming pines begin to look a lot like prison bars. Episodic perils abound: shoot-outs with vagrants, dodging timber in a downriver log drive and a heart-in-throat crossing over a groaning rope bridge that owes a debt to the infamously hair-raising sequence in William Friedkin’s Sorcerer . McKinley stages the action with stripped-down grit, but there’s a horror director in the making here. Set to a strobing lightning storm, the callous killing of a wounded member is genuinely unnerving.

Eventually, the weight of the title becomes clear. It’s not the gold. It’s the pain each convict is carrying, revealed in walk-and-talk backstories. Sadly, only two characters register: oily snake Rankin (Austin Amelio) and indigenous runaway Anna (Julia Jones, formidable until a needless romance). Crowe is clearly in Dark Mode after playing Goring in Nuremberg . Clancy — a glowering, tobacco-spitting mood tyrant — is another ripe addition to his growing villain gallery, brief though it is. Ignore the top-billing: he’s a bookend to Murphy’s journey.

This is Hawke’s vehicle, and his dogged presence drives the film. Those once boyish features are hardening into a crag of weathered rock. The eyes are as soulful as ever, though, and the role of grizzled hero fits him like a dirty glove. Weirdly, the credits run a smiley you’ve-been-watching cast roll-call to Lynyrd Skynyrd. Great for a cast-and-crew screening, but it pulls you right out of the desolate mood.
review_summary: Bleak, stark and ruthless, this survival thriller falls short on heart-in-mouth peril, but an exceptional Ethan Hawke is all-in as a broken man clawing towards salvation.

about_movie: After his daughter is kidnapped, a mute father (Xie Miao) and a journalist (Joe Taslim) go on the warpath to take down a child-trafficking ring.
review:
As the blood-soaked final showdown of The Furious unfolds, you will start to notice that across its near two-hour runtime there are barely five minutes of this film where someone isn’t being punched, kicked, or having their face slammed through a table. It’s clearly where action choreographer-turned-director Kenji Tanigaki is most comfortable, and considering the kidnapped-daughter plot here boils down to a repackaged version of_Taken_ , it’s a good thing. Thankfully, Tanigaki trusts his instincts, getting his characters to shut up and play the hits, throws, and bone-breaking blows, resulting in a relentlessly fun slice of Hong Kong martial-arts mayhem.

There’s real creativity in how the action escalates. It begins with mute father Wang Wei (Xie Miao) attempting to rescue his kidnapped daughter in a surprisingly blood-light slice of Jackie Chan-inspired (notably First Strike ) kung fu, which sees the performers creatively throwing themselves in, around, and through a truck. From there, the film continually ups the ante, eventually arriving at a wall-painting police-station brawl that mixes wushu, judo and more to unleash absolute carnage that wouldn’t feel out of place in the Raid films. It’s made more immersive by sound design that ensures you feel every damn crunch, heightened further by Tanigaki’s camera, which weaves through every fight with the kind of energy that feels like it’s just downed a Red Bull. Throw in the electronic score, and this is pretty jaw-dropping (or snapping) stuff.

Elsewhere, the action embraces complete absurdity. Want to see a child riding down a hallway on the back of a motorbike while whacking henchmen? This is the movie for you. It’s all played with a not-so-subtle wink —the kind of bananas action to which you sense somehow, somewhere John Woo is raising a glass.

The Furious clearly isn’t afraid to go over the top. In true Hong Kong tradition, its emotions are running just as high as the number of bodies hitting the floor. The film’s attempts at emotional moments with journalist Navin (Joe Taslim), who joins Wang Wei on the mission, don’t always land quite as well as the punches, but its commitment to emulating Hong Kong classics is admirable. The same can be said for its child-centred drama, which slows the plot slightly as it enters its final act. Thankfully, the film quickly remembers what everyone is really here for.

The showstopper comes in the form of a mid-movie fight, featuring Everything Everywhere All At Once ’s Brian Le. The martial artist swaps butt plugs for a sledgehammer, an absolutely dominating screen presence as he towers over Xie and Taslim. The trio blast their way through a warehouse, trading one inventive blow after another as the hammer swings between them, changes hands, and even smashes through human ice sculptures (with actual humans inside — as disgusting as that sounds!) to create an even bloodier mess. For a brief moment, you might find yourself thinking that all this insanity is exactly what cinema was made for.

The Furious wears all its influences proudly on its sleeve, but comparisons aside, Kenji Tanigaki has still created a bone-crunching beast that feels distinctly his own. More of this mayhem, please.
review_summary: Tipping its hat to countless Hong Kong classics, this is a relentlessly entertaining martial-arts epic that knows exactly what its audience wants, landing enough blows to leave you suitably floored.

about_movie: Nick (Kit Connor) and Charlie (Joe Locke) are as in love as ever. But it’s the final year of sixth form, and Nick’s impending move to university and Charlie’s new role as head boy deliver a new set of obstacles that threaten to topple their seemingly insurmountable romance.
review:
Debuting in 2022, Heartstopper — based on the graphic novels of the same name by Alice Oseman — was the rare TV series that didn’t sideline its queer characters, instead allowing them to thrive in the spotlight as protagonists. More than that, the show (also written by Oseman) has always highlighted queer joy, a tonic to the overwhelming number of stories about LGBTQ+ people rooted in trauma.

Though the show is widely celebrated, it has garnered its fair share of criticism for being twee and overly wholesome. That’s a critique Heartstopper Forever , the feature-length film that doubles as the series finale, hasclearly internalised. Written by Oseman and directed by Wash Westmoreland (who previously directed Colette , a film which makes a cameo appearance here), this is Heartstopper at its most mature. There’s less of the heart-fluttering whimsy that dominated the series, though this is especially impressive in how it balances heavy topics like sex (of which there’s plenty), anxiety, and self-harm with the show’s trademark charm.

We re-join Nick (Kit Connor) and Charlie ( Joe Locke ) at a major transition point. Because Charlie’s a year younger, Nick will be off to university before him, and he’s chosen Leeds, a considerable distance from Kent. More concerning is that Nick is in crisis over his upcoming departure. Long-distance is a major challenge for any relationship, and they both know it. Nick has spent so much time caring for Charlie as he struggled with an eating disorder and self-harm that he’s lost sight of who he is; to cope with it, he’s started to depend on alcohol. Heartstopper may be known for a light touch, but it deals with their conflicts with a striking sincerity. This is a film that explores the idea of soulmates, and how despite loving each other so much, you can lose sight of what’s right in front of you.

Such is the focus on the main couple that if you’re hoping for any big storylines from anyone but Nick and Charlie, you’ll likely be disappointed. There are lovely moments involving Elle (Yasmin Finney) and Isaac (Tobie Donovan), which neatly wrap up their stories, but Heartstopper has always been about Nick and Charlie, and Oseman’s script does wonderful work with the pair. Both Connor and Locke deliver the finest performances of their young careers; their chemistry feels lived-in and authentic, lending tremendous heft to the film’s sweet and hard-hitting moments.

Movingly, Heartstopper Forever is also acutely aware of the show’s impact — there’s a touching plotline on the impact Charlie has had on a younger student for being proudly and openly gay, a fitting avatar for everyone who’s been affected by the show. Westmoreland’s film is an apt send-off for these characters, a more complex and humane version of Heartstopper than was found in the series.
review_summary: Heartstopper Forever ups the ante with a heartwarming and honest finale for Nick, Charlie and the gang. Get those tissues ready.

about_movie: After victory in the Trojan War, Odysseus (Matt Damon) spends years struggling to return home to his wife Penelope (Anne Hathaway) and son Telemachus (Tom Holland). Will the gods allow it?
review:
The Odyssey is the definition of epic. The word comes from the Ancient Greek epikos , an adjective used to describe a long narrative, prophecy, proverb or heroic verse. All such interpretations could describe Homer’s vast 8th-century BC poem, a masterwork of Greek mythology, about a bloke just trying to get home — the Planes, Trains And Automobiles of the Bronze Age, if you will. It is a 12,000-line, 24-book, 3,000-year-old piece of literature, a journey of gods and monsters, spanning many years, across seas and islands, over warring lands and into the underworld itself.

Fairly ambitious, then. Christopher Nolan, of course, is hardly a stranger to ambition: his first major film, Memento , was told both backwards and forwards, and he has tackled wars, superheroes, dreams, wormholes, the nuclear apocalypse and Victorian teleportation machines. But it’s not unreasonable to suggest that The Odyssey is his most ambitious film yet. Set in a “time of apparent magic”, as the opening title card has it, we dive headfirst into a world of both divine fantasy and grounded realism. From the start, the story here is dense with plot and detail, sometimes seemingly explained by a character called Expositionus.

Still, it is as elegant and economical an adaptation as it’s possible to make of such a lengthy tome, and you don’t need a Classics degree to understand it. Some purists may bristle at the liberties taken with the text, with significant omissions (Odysseus accidentally opens a bag of wind! Odysseus competes in a sports day!). The dialogue, too, inevitably loses some of the poetry and lyricism of the original text; no dactylic hexameter here. But what it loses in faithfulness, it gains in visual and structural poetry. It is a beautifully edited film, Nolan taking Homer’s flashback structure and running with it, telling a story in nesting narratives. Sometimes you can only tell how far along on the journey you are from the grey in Matt Damon’s beard.

This is a film thickly packed with incident, the kind that may only truly be fully appreciated through repeat viewings. After efficiently introducing the world, we watch Odysseus (Damon) and his increasingly unfortunate band of merry men encounter a Cyclops (staggering and grotesque), Sirens (haunting and sad), and the giant Laestrygonians (featuring the most upsetting child acting this side of an Omen movie). Much has been made of Nolan’s love of practical effects, but what is most impressive during these extraordinary set-pieces — all soundtracked to Ludwig Göransson’s experimentally pulsing score — is the integration of techniques, blending puppetry, stunt performers, special effects and — yes! — CGI so seamlessly as to make this mythic world feel real.

The scale and scope here is, frankly, jaw-detaching. It is filmmaking at a magnitude few modern directors could ever realistically imagine, demand, or execute. Yet what is most striking about this film is its quieter moments. The gods here are human-sized: the fury of Zeus and Poseidon is felt only in the elements, while Calypso (Charlize Theron) simply wants a companion, and Athena (Zendaya, doing much with little, in a role strikingly similar to the one she played in the first Dune ) is seen only in flashes of an enigmatic half-dream — or perhaps as a trauma-response. Samantha Morton’s Circe, meanwhile, provides the closest Nolan has come to full-on horror, an astonishing sequence full of shocking fury and sadness at the baseness of men.

As it was in the text, the heroes of this tale are mere humans, full of flaws and foibles. Damon, by now a Nolan regular, embodies Odysseus brilliantly and bravely, as a weary soldier burdened by the weight of leadership and his vast, Scylla-and-Charybdis-sized trolley problems. Nolan emphasises his fallibility; on more than one occasion, our champion is forced to leg it back to his boat in the manner of Monty Python ’s King Arthur (“Run away!”).

It is in the final act, when Odysseus finally makes it back to Ithaca, reunites with son Telemachus (Tom Holland, solid) and wife Penelope (Anne Hathaway, fierce) and confronts the boorish suitors led by Antinous (Robert Pattinson, chewing scenery delightfully), that the film comes into focus. Greece is spoken of as the “greatest civilisation the world has ever seen”, a fading empire policing and colonising the world, and Nolan seems to embrace parallels with American exceptionalism and Manifest Destiny; the accents adopted by the cast cements this point. (Make Ithaca Great Again?)

By his journey’s end, Odysseus seems heartbroken at the state of the world, and his role in its downfall. There is something of Powell & Pressburger’s The Life And Death Of Colonel Blimp in its coda, in a military man mourning the death of honour, as well as echoes as Nolan’s own work: like Dunkirk , it laments the absurdity and pointlessness of war, and like Oppenheimer , it trembles at the catastrophic failures of a great and terrible man. It may be set in a mythical universe, but Nolan is again raging at the folly of a humanity we might recognise — on an enormous, IMAX-sized canvas. Nobody does it better.
review_summary: A worthy new translation of an ancient text, and yet another monumental piece of work from one of our boldest filmmakers. Watch it on the most colossal screen you can find.

about_movie: Following a viral apocalypse, Hig (Jacob Elordi) survives by scavenging supplies with his dog and flying a small plane around from a remote airfield where he lives with Bangley (Josh Brolin). As the threats grow, he attempts to fly further in search of civilisation — but it won’t be easy.
review:
Post-apocalyptic films aim to reduce us to our essence, to make us question what, in the end, we need to hold onto and who we can’t live without. Ridley Scott’s latest also tries to go deeper, to examine the difference between surviving and thriving. The only problem is that it doesn’t seem entirely convinced of its own answers.

Jacob Elordi stars as Hig, an everyday guy who’s just trying to get by in the newly depopulated America. With his dog, Jasper, he flies scavenging missions into Denver and brings back supplies for his companion at the airfield where he lives, the warlike Bangley ( Josh Brolin ). But there are signs of “reapers” in the city, semi-feral gangs that steal from other survivors, and they could threaten both men and their Mennonite neighbours. And when Hig sets off to chase a faint radio signal he’s heard from Grand Junction, he faces new friendships and new threats.

Scott shot the film in Italy, and the jagged teeth of the Dolomites lend the scenery an appropriately threatening edge. Cinematographer Erik Messerschmidt’s aerial photography is glorious (nominative determinism at work?), as Hig soars between peaks entirely devoid of humanity. The now 88-year-old Scott shoots action with an energy that filmmakers half his age struggle to match, and has assembled an enviably talented cast. The issue is more that the narrative fails to match his drive, sunk in the same fug as these depressive characters. There's only so much magnetism a cast can emit when in a state of near-suicidal resignation.

The first half has an effective sense of threat, albeit from a particularly ill-defined and confusingly portrayed group, but given that characters make bizarre decisions like lighting fires in the wilderness for all to see, it's not clear if they're as worried as we are. Then things slow to a crawl to half-cook a new relationship for Hig and plucky survivor Cima (Margaret Qualley). And there are the abrupt and at times bewildering shifts of tone. One deeply odd sequence at an airport, an addition to the book, belongs in an entirely different emotional universe — or maybe nowhere at all. It might have been an attempt to pep things up, but it's misguided.

Still, you understand the impulse to add some zing. Little here feels fresh; perhaps because its 2012 source novel, by Peter Heller, has inspired other work since, or perhaps because it coincidentally shares elements with other, better stories. There’s the loyal dog of I Am Legend , the manic berserkers of Mad Max (though without their wit or characterisation) and even the bonkers future-nostalgia of Fallout at one point. Such common touchpoints wouldn’t be a problem if the resulting film hung together, but this one does not; it doesn't seem quite sure what it wants to say. There's a touch more hope at the end than at the beginning, with a new reason for Hig to keep living and a new outlook on life, but even that largely relies on him appreciating what he already had rather than any fundamental change in his circumstances. The film wants to thrive, but it's barely surviving.
review_summary: It’s a beautiful, mountainous spin on the post-apocalyptic genre, but too familiar and too downbeat to really stick in the mind.

about_movie: Teenage punks Tommy (Mason Thames), Fred (Kylr Coffman) and Chad (Ryan Foust) make an ill-advised road trip across America in the mistaken belief that they are the support act for legendary pop-punk band Green Day.
review:
If you are a fan of the ’90s pop-punk heroes, Nimrods is a major work. This film is very much an extension of the Green Day brand: the band as a collective have “produced by” and “story by” credits and the story is heavily inspired by their early years as struggling musicians on the road, before they became Millennial pop-punk heroes. The plot revolves around three obsessive Green Day fans, and Green Day also star as themselves, the film culminating in a gig in which multiple classic Green Day songs are performed.

That might suggest strictly-for-fans-only territory — but what is surprising about Nimrods (which previously carried the title ‘New Year's Rev’) is how accessible and charming it manages to be. It’s directed by Lee Kirk, who ten years ago directed Green Day lead singer Billie Joe Armstrong in the semi-fictional film Ordinary World . The filmmaker clearly has a lot of love and affection for the band, but this story trains the focus on its young cast, Green Day acolytes loosely based on the band members themselves.

Our three scruffy heroes here are rebellious truant Tommy ( The Black Phone ’s Mason Thames), green-haired masturbator Fred (Kylr Coffman), and bespectacled “narc” Chad (Ryan Foust), who the other two lambast for being too reliable (“If you want to be a punk rocker, you’ve got to be late!”). Tapping into the Gen-Z obsession with ’90s nostalgia, these three are obsessed with Green Day and juvenilia of that era: their band, in fact, is called Analog Dogs (they get repeatedly mistakenly pronounced as “Anal OG Dogs”), and they delight in recording demos on a four-track and filming their punky exploits on an old-school camcorder.

Kirk reflects this in his filming style, shooting Kansas City grungily and grainily as a kind of suburban Nowheresville, USA. After a prank goes wrong, the band incorrectly believe they are supporting Green Day at their headline New Year’s Eve gig in Los Angeles, and scrabble together whatever resources they can to make the journey West — along the way meeting all manner of colourful characters, including indie-cool love interest Olivia (Mckenna Grace) and an eccentric motel owner (Fred Armisen).

Along the way, the familiar formula of a coming-of-age road-trip can be keenly felt. Some comic interludes — Fred takes mushrooms; hijinx ensue — land a little too broadly, and you find yourself wishing that the characters had been fleshed out a touch more. The looming absence of Tommy’s late father is the only real emotional backstory we get.

So, it’s scrappy and a little rough around the edges. You sense that’s exactly how Green Day would like it. The film’s heart and sincerity are never in doubt, and if the ending is predictable, it’s nothing less than sweet and triumphant. And if you are a Green Day fan — or at the very least had working ears during the 1990s and early 2000s — you will be cheered by the excess of the band’s anthems on the soundtrack: of course mournful ballad ‘Wake Me Up When September Ends’ plays during a key second-act turning point! Of course ‘Good Riddance (Time Of Your Life)’ plays as the film ends! For all its faults, Nimrods is a joyful expression of what it means to be young. While listening, crucially, to Green Day.
review_summary: Do you have the time, to listen to this film whine, about nothing and everything all at once? If so, you’ll be rewarded with a mostly successful coming-of-age teenage ode to punk.

about_movie: In a sleepy small-town community, a mysterious Ice Cream Man (Ari Millen) sells his frozen desserts to unsuspecting children. Soon, they are under his spell – and murdering all the adults.
review:
There has been a vibe shift. And Eli Roth has been left behind. In the early 2000s, he was the enfant terrible of horror, a cine-savvy sadistic-splatter specialist who tapped into something cool and transgressive. Today, the landscape looks very different: horror films are now winning Oscars, outgrossing major franchises at the box office, and rich with grown-up themes. Ice Cream Man — a sugary riff on Children Of The Corn (Children Of The Cone?) — is Roth’s latest attempt to go back to his gory roots. After some odd recent diversions (the family-friendly fantasy The House With A Clock In Its Walls , the abysmal video-game adaptation Borderlands ), it seems, along with 2023’s Thanksgiving , like a deliberate throwback to his noughties heyday, full of the gleeful gore and goofy tone that defined his biggest hits ( Cabin Fever , Hostel ).

But in every sense, this film feels out of time and place. The most exciting voices in horror are now 20-somethings from YouTube — the Philippous, the Barkers and the Parsons of the world. The torture-porn market has been sewn up by Damien Leone’s Terrifier series, which does practical effects more imaginatively and gruesomely than this. Even the very idea of ‘kids being possessed and turned into weapons’ has been recently executed far better, and more interestingly, in, erm, Zach Cregger’s Weapons .

So, what are we left with? Well, first and foremost, a bloodthirsty premise. Indeed, that seems to be the only thing actually considered here, at the expense of almost everything else. It’s a straightforward genre conceit: a creepily cheery, pencil-moustached, Pee-wee Herman-esque ice cream vendor (Ari Millen, blameless) rolls into town one day and distributes ice cream to the community’s young population. Soon they become murderous zombies, who bend only to the never-speaking Ice Cream Man’s will. Cue an unremitting parade of crazy kills, performed by children too young to even get into a 12A.

Pretty standard stuff, but Roth seems to have arrived at his concept, his opportunity to indulge in a bit of bloody butchery, without ever properly thinking about a story, compelling characters, or even vaguely plausible dialogue. Scenes meander from A to B with no particular flow or motivation. Characters have no arcs, inner lives, or even discernible traits, beyond being fodder for death, or running away from it. The script is a genuinely head-scratching cobbled-together collection of sub-Joss Whedon attempts at wit. (At one point, a pre-teen child references the 1992 film Glengarry Glen Ross — because kids love Mamet, right?)

If you’re simply here for relentless, unthinking ultraviolence, you’ll be satisfied enough, sure. But it’s gore for the sake of gore. There is no care for actual story or character beats. No unfortunate soul is established well enough for us to ever care when they inevitably meet their grisly demise. At one point, a fireman comes to rescue the kids; naturally they smash his face in with bricks. Then, a paramedic is dragged along behind his own ambulance, to the screaming cheers of the zombie-fied children. Forget poetic justice, the film seems to say — it’s about time the emergency services get taken down a peg or two!

Roth’s horror films have always delighted in the nasty, but here the filmmaking feels genuinely unpleasant, even beyond the blood-and-guts stuff.  Some characters are openly sexist (“Chicks are expensive!” muses one of our heroes). There is a casual use of an ableist slur, and a horrible, horrible ‘joke’ about bulimia, from a 12-year-old. That’s not even to mention the unforgivably anti-art use of glaringly obvious generative AI, across multiple sequences. If you can’t be bothered to hire human artists for your cheap, shallow, unthinking gore-fest, what are we even doing here?
review_summary: Ugly, unpleasant and utterly insubstantial, this ice cream just leaves a bad taste in the mouth.

about_movie: Nineteen-year-old Anthony Bourdain (Dominic Sessa) finds himself spending the summer working in a small Provincetown restaurant under the tutelage of a local chef (Antonio Banderas).
review:
How exactly do you make a film about Anthony Bourdain? He was a gargantuan figure, one of the most famous chefs in history, a man who proved how a $6 bowl of noodles could break down barriers between those who feel worlds apart. From his time in New York’s culinary underbelly to getting blackout drunk on the streets of Seoul, no film could ever fully encapsulate the man’s life or find the time to reckon with the complex legacy he left behind. Matt Johnson’s biopic Tony is far less interested in painting a whole picture (look to the excellent documentary Roadrunner: A Film About Anthony Bourdain for that) and instead focuses on one summer from the opening chapters of his acclaimed memoir Kitchen Confidential , when Bourdain spent a summer cooking in the coastal resort of Provincetown, Massachusetts.

It quickly becomes clear that Tony is a hangout movie. Wandering into parts unknown after failing to secure a writing scholarship and chasing a girl (an incredibly underserved Emilia Jones), Dominic Sessa’s Bourdain is aimless, full of misplaced confidence, and a barefaced liar. To be frank, he’s a bit of a dick. Dominic Sessa can do this sort of thing in his sleep. Much of his performance here feels like an extension of his role in The Holdovers , always entertaining but not revolutionary. While it never feels like he fully steps into the personality of the famous chef, you can see some of the DNA there.

What feels most alive here is Provincetown. From bustling parties to late-night cookouts, it’s a film that mostly lets you soak in its summer. For the most part, Johnson’s hands feel very light on this film — no Nirvanna The Band The Show The Movie shenanigans here — but it’s in the kitchen where his style feels most prominent, capturing chaotic acts of chef hedonism that play like vignettes of a summer that won’t soon be forgotten.

It’s a shame, then, that for all the culinary excellence on display, Tony ’s exploration of food doesn’t extend beyond Antonio Banderas’ head chef. The film never really does the work to allow us to understand why Bourdain was eventually won over by this world. That disconnect leaves much of its third act feeling adrift. In the end, those wanting to see an icon immortalised on screen may not leave fully satiated.

However, it’s hard not to be reeled in by the quintessential Bourdain charm of taking in a culture and its people. “Travel changes you,” the man himself once wrote. “As you move through this life and this world you change things slightly, you leave marks behind, however small. And in return, life — and travel — leaves marks on you.” Johnson’s film never fully captures the man Bourdain became, but in appropriate fashion it finds its story in the people and the place that left their mark on him.
review_summary: A hangout movie is perhaps the most fitting way for Bourdain to be brought to the screen. Though its ambitions never quite match its subject, it depicts a summer you’ll be hard-pressed not to be charmed by.

about_movie: After an injury, former tennis pro Dusty Boyd (Jake Johnson) has to pivot to pickleball — causing friction with his domineering dad (Ed Harris).
review:
You don’t need to have picked up the broad, light paddle used for pickleball to know what a sporting phenomenon it’s become in recent years. Its selling-point? Essentially anyone can play it. Hence its mounting popularity among the elderly, the very young, and anyone who might want to avoid the pace and rigour of tennis, pickleball’s racier peer. Of course, if you like tennis, pickleball may feel like playing your preferred sport in a vat of hummus. Which is the predicament Dusty Boyd (Jake Johnson) finds himself in. He’s a fallen-prodigy-turned-tennis-coach, who after an injury is encouraged to build back his strength on a different kind of court, one frequented by those partial to a fanny pack and early-bird special.

The Dodgeball comparisons to The Dink are inevitable: a leftfield sport and an average Joe hero (Dusty is a corny showman who, underneath the bravado, longs for the approval of his pickleball-loathing pops). Ben Stiller even shows up as Dusty’s doctor. It’s got undeniable comedy chops behind the camera as well, courtesy of Barb And Star Go To Vista Del Mar filmmaker Josh Greenbaum. Yet rather than being a clean-cut David and Goliath story, The Dink instead finds its strength in the partnership of Dusty and his reluctant teammate Candace, played with boundless charm by Mary Steenburgen.

The script leans towards that frat-pack brand of humour from the era of Stiller, Owen Wilson and co., with Johnson the immature underdog, all pageantry and insults shielding the wildly insecure and misdirected person underneath. The gags, however, have a recycled feel to them, and distract from Johnson’s better qualities, his strongest being connecting with his co-stars with a jovial ease. When he and Steenburgen are in hangout mode, trading playlists and watching movies, we get a glimpse of the movie that could have been: a sweet double act that would be satisfying whether it becomes romantic or not. It’s rare that we get to see Steenburgen in a larger supporting role and so when the story inevitably tapers to a pickleball showdown (although less obviously between Dusty and former tennis star Andy Roddick, playing himself), and Candace is ushered courtside, you really feel the loss of her twinkling presence. The central thrust of the plot — Dusty must win the tournament in order to appease his grouchy father (Ed Harris) and save his country club — just isn’t as strong.

There’s still plenty that makes this a pleasing popcorn movie: foul-mouthed pensioners, a couple of decent cameos, as much action as you’re going to squeeze out of a game where the ball is full of small holes. Yet bar the joyful chemistry between its top-billing talent, the script does little to nudge The Dink over the line.
review_summary: Despite reaching for the oddball energy of sports comedies past, this movie is best when Johnson and Steenburgen are given room to play off the court. Let the pickleball watch from the sidelines instead!

about_movie: Family ties — which are closer than most — are tested when eldest brother Jack (Jamie Bell) tries to bring his new girlfriend Martha (Elle Fanning) into the fold.
review:
Efthimis Filippou has been responsible for some of Yorgos Lanthimos’ darkest material, co-writing most of the Oscar-winner’s bleak satirical oeuvre ( Dogtooth , The Lobster , and Kinds Of Kindness to name but a few.) With this Catalonia-set family affair he continues his provocative streak, penning the screenplay for a gaudy, hollow study of a wealthy father and children’s taboo inner workings inspired by Marco Bellocchio’s Italian ’65 classic Fists In The Pocket .

Director Karim Aïnouz shepherds a heavyweight cast through the film’s thorny heart, which finds the relocated family patched back together after the violent death of their mother (Pamela Anderson), killed by wolves. Now, they face further upheaval as Jack (Jamie Bell), the family pillar, attempts to unstick himself from his socially aloof father (Tracy Letts) and rabid grown-up siblings, while introducing his girlfriend Martha (Elle Fanning).

Of the horny brood, Callum Turner is a standout as the periphery-hovering, Ripley -type middle brother Ed, as is Riley Keough as their entertainingly petulant sister Anna. Upon learning that Martha is a gifted guitarist, Anna brings out her own guitar to strum in an act of churlish defiance. The film is spotted with these wry moments, which feel earned amid the wretched dynamic of the ensemble, mostly shown from the perspectives of Jack and Ed — the former determined to start life anew at a violent price, the latter sinking further into domestic dysfunction to a shocking degree.

Yet the stilted material is too committed to shock and opulence at a time when eat-the-rich fables are already at cat-swinging capacity. The ensemble’s collective vapidness is taken too literally, with the script never bothering to dip below the surface and interrogate the messy, sad malaise just out of sight. Instead, we’re encouraged to float, satisfied, in the film’s sea of catwalk-ready costumes, alluring architecture, overworked metaphors and strangely sterile brutality. Even with the body-count rising, however, fluids and flora are not enough to make this rosebush rise above the rest.
review_summary: This dark comedy’s aesthetic glossiness seeps over the story’s jagged edges, leaving a smooth, glassy and impenetrable movie with nothing new to say.

about_movie: In Paris, a spiralling psychotherapist (Foster) suspects one of her patients may have been murdered.
review:
While film and television history has made way for a plethora of onscreen therapists — from Robin Williams in Good Will Hunting to Lorraine Bracco in The Sopranos — it was once relatively rare for shrinks to achieve main-character status. Between last year’s Rose-Byrne-starring If I Had Legs I’d Kick You and, now, delightful sleuthing-shrink dramedy A Private Life , therapists themselves finally seem to be the ones on the psychoanalysis couch.

After her exquisite parenthood romcom Other People’s Children , French filmmaker Rebecca Zlotowski reunites with Virginie Efira, who here plays another mother who may or may not have been murdered. But the effortless charisma of Efira (even when playing a corpse) aside, A Private Life is undeniably a performance vehicle for its American lead, Jodie Foster, who finds herself again somewhat in The Silence Of The Lambs mode, as a shrink-turned-amateur-detective.

Foster’s Dr Lilian Steiner lives in a Paris apartment of dreams. The Jewish therapist is frequently slagged off by her neighbours, her fed-up patients are steadily ditching her, and, after her client Paula (Efira) dies, this usually stoic professional starts crying unstoppably for the first time in years.

At first glance, this seems like a clear-cut meltdown. Yet after Lilian is approached by Paula’s daughter Valérie (Luàna Bajrami), the analyst gets wind that something about her departed former patient’s family is off. Convinced by a quack hypnotist that these events are an elaborate case of déjà vu, Lilian digs further, enlisting the help of her eye-doctor ex Gabriel (Daniel Auteuil) — much to the ire of her unimpressed son Julien (Vincent Lacoste) — and trotting around the French capital with a voice recorder à la Twin Peaks .

Visually, A Private Life is très chic. Georges Lechaptois’ cinematography, Katia Wyszkop’s production design and Bénédicte Mouret’s costuming combine for an aesthetic feast. Below this gloss, though, Zlotowski, Anne Berest and Gaëlle Macé’s screenplay is somewhat slight. There are some standout scenes, such as a comic chaise-longue montage, a wild hypnotherapy dream sequence and a sequence with a tuxedoed Foster which seems to parallel TÁR . But overall, this story of a doctor seeking to cure her ennui is thin in terms of its theme of Jewish identity, and has an unsteady denouement.

That does not detract from the fun of the ride, however. French-film fans will be pleased with its stellar Gallic ensemble — especially Quantum Of Solace ’s Mathieu Amalric, who makes an excellent villain — elevated to new levels by the brilliance of Foster, who adeptly navigates this twisty world. And — a fluent speaker, having attended a lycée as a child — she does it all in impeccable French.
review_summary: This stylish, silly and strange whodunnit/family-drama mash-up, while shaky at times, is a fun filmic amuse-bouche, with Foster on top form.

about_movie: Enola Holmes (Millie Bobby Brown), now officially a detective, heads to Malta to marry her beloved Lord Tewkesbury (Louis Partridge). However, the nuptials are put on hold when Enola’s brother Sherlock (Henry Cavill) goes missing, setting in motion the young sleuth’s most dangerous case to date.
review:
Having brought us one of the darkest, boldest, and most talked-about things to hit our screens in 2025, one-shot child-killer series Adolescence , it would be fair to say it came as something of a surprise when Netflix announced that director-writer duo Philip Barantini and Jack Thorne’s next team-up would be on the newest Enola Holmes movie. But while Enola Holmes 3 never threatens to be anything as groundbreaking as Adolescence (which, in fairness, was never its MO), this third instalment in the adventures of Sherlock Holmes’ sleuthing younger sister is far from elementary. For both better and worse.

To give a sense of how many plates Barantini and Thorne are spinning with Netflix’s latest dive into the world of Nancy Springer’s wildly popular books, consider this. In the first ten minutes of the movie there is *deep breath* a jailbreak plot, a ‘one year later’ time jump-forward, a ‘some months earlier’ time jump-back, a horse-drawn-carriage chase, both the beginning of a wedding and then the proposal (in that order), the reveal that Henry Cavill’s Sherlock Holmes is missing, and some plot-pertinent exposition relating to the Explosive Substances Act of 1883. Oh, and everyone heads off to Malta for Enola Holmes’ (Millie Bobby Brown) and Lord Viscount Earnest Augustus Tewkesbury’s (Louis Partridge) nuptials. And yet somehow — somehow — this third sister-sleuther caper is nearly half an hour shorter than Enola Holmes 2 . (Which, in almost any other circumstance, would actually be a blessed relief.)

By the time you chuck in a spot of ‘Sins Of The British Empire For Dummies’ courtesy of a band of Maltese freedom-fighters and the return of Sharon Duncan-Brewster’s deliciously well-pitched but ultimately still fairly inert Moriarty, what you end up with is a high-octane adventure that is occasionally breathless, often exhausting, but admittedly never boring.

Working in Enola Holmes 3 ’s favour right from the jump is the fact that, despite blamelessly both possessing iPhone faces (Google it), Millie Bobby Brown and Louis Partridge’s chemistry remains as effortless here as it has been from that first film six years ago. Sure, Enola and Tewkesbury’s loggerheads-to-lovers love story isn’t really anything new to YA readers, or anyone who’s ever watched a teen romance, for that matter. But there’s a surprisingly rich exploration of co-dependence here — and what marriage may do to Enola’s identity, which she’s struggled so hard to forge — that allows Brown and Partridge to add new steps to Enola and Tewkesbury’s now-familiar dance. A particularly lovely oceanside sequence between the pair, a moment of (re)connection amid the chaos of everything around them, is so sincerely romantic and beautifully played that it’s almost a shame when it ends and the overarching plot kicks back in.

The thing is that there’s actually no shortage of elements to recommend Enola Holmes 3 . Costume designer Consolata Boyle has outdone herself with the various incredible fits on display here, all intricately detailed and impeccably tailored finery that's sure to spawn a thousand cosplays. It’s also incredibly well-lit and dynamically shot by Barantini’s Boiling Point and Adolescence cinematographer Matt Lewis. (Seriously, never underestimate the amount of goodwill generated by a bit of decent lighting in the streaming age.) The film’s social commentary — on the legacy of empire (British, not our magazine), on gender and class and the weight of familial legacy — is as well-handled as you'd expect from a Thorne script. And Barantini even manages to squeeze in a couple of signature oners that, though comparatively low-key when weighed against his past works, give this entry a kinetic force that sets it apart from its predecessors.

The actual problem with this third film, then, is simply that it’s just so overstuffed, knotty and overly plotty that it rarely gives itself (or the viewer) chance to take stock and catch breath. There are great moments — the above-mentioned oceanside rendezvous; an unexpected heart-to-heart between Watson (an underused but ever-dependable Himesh Patel) and Tewkesbury; a Maltese-flavoured third-act Mexican stand-off — but they’re bound to a story that constantly feels as if it’s creaking under the weight of its many moving parts. By the time the credits roll, it’s hard to fully remember everything the past 105 minutes have held, let alone make sense of some of it. Still, it’s all fun and game’s afoot while it lasts.
review_summary: Millie Bobby Brown’s third outing as Sherlock Holmes’ maverick, mystery-solving kid sister may be messy, and more than a little convoluted, but it’s a fine caper nonetheless.

about_movie: Finn (Roman Griffin Davis) and his younger brother Charlie (Dexter Sol Ansell) have run away from home. They have a plan: travel from Sheffield to the small seaside town of Dingle, Ireland, to reunite with their estranged grandfather (Bill Nighy) in a bid to bring their family back together.
review:
“If you asked me where we were happiest, I’d say here, in Dingle. I suppose I thought it would always be like that,” Finn (Roman Griffin Davis) narrates at the beginning of Morgan Matthews’ tender road-trip tear-jerker 500 Miles (which, despite the title, is not a Proclaimers musical á la Sunshine On Leith ). It’s easy to see what Finn’s getting at: when we meet them in a flashback, it’s a picture-perfect day for Finn and his family, sharing special moments on the beach with his grandparents, playing boules and building sandcastles.

Those moments are just a memory. In the present day, Finn and Charlie (Dexter Sol Ansell) no longer have a relationship with their grandfather (Bill Nighy, who tells us everything we need to know with his eyes). Their grandmother has passed away, and their parents are constantly bickering. Sneaking out of their home, the brothers decide to embark on an ill-advised road trip, from Sheffield to the west coast of Ireland, to track down their grandfather and reunite the family. Their journey won’t be an easy one, as they’re too young to travel without adult supervision, and Matthews’ clever framing reminds us how vast the countryside is, hills and mountains dwarfing their small frames. Their journey gets a surprise assist from Kait (a lovely Maisie Williams), who they meet on a train while she is busking.

There’s a wonderfully authentic relationship between Finn and Charlie at the heart of 500 Miles . As Finn, Davis is terrific, continuing to impress after his breakthrough performance in Jojo Rabbit . Ansell, best known for his role in A Knight Of The Seven Kingdoms , is delightful as Charlie, managing to toe a tricky line of feeling both larger-than-life and authentically grounded. It’s always a risk to anchor your film on child performances, but Finn and Charlie’s brotherly love is likely to remind you of your relationship with your own siblings.

The film hinges on a reveal that, once unveiled, shifts everything into a new perspective. Whether it works for you will likely define how you feel about the movie: if you’re averse to heavy doses of sentimentality, then you’ll probably wind up annoyed. And this film is drenched in sentimentality. But while 500 Miles can feel cloying and heavy-handed — a relentless, overbearing score doesn’t help — it’s hard not to be moved by it, thanks to the wonderful work of its two leads.
review_summary: Though 500 Miles tries too hard to wring tears from your eyes, knockout performances by the film’s two young actors sustain this emotional and surprising road trip.
