about_movie: Framed for the murder of his billionaire boss, bodyguard Cole Reed (Jason Statham) boards a shipping vessel and there uncovers an international conspiracy as he fights to clear his name.
review:
From the writer (J.P. Davis) and director (Jean-François Richet) of Plane , this action-thriller is reported to have begun life as a sequel to that 2023 Gerard Butler vehicle. It was entitled, naturally, ‘ Ship ’, but retooled after Butler, well, jumped ship, thus clearing the way for Jason Statham to board a movie that might be described as Die Hard On A Boat, had Under Siege not got there already. Thirty-four years ago.

Mutiny is a throwback, the kind of contained, no-nonsense action picture that Hollywood thrived on before CGI made anything possible… except, in most cases, realism and peril. Statham has previously played getaway drivers, bank robbers, cops, hitmen, construction workers and a beekeeper, but nearly all of his tough guys are ex-somethings, and so it is here. In fact, bodyguard Cole Reed is doubly hard because he’s an ex-cop and an ex-Royal Marine (“I pissed off the wrong people”). He’s also a master strategist, always three moves ahead. We know this because, early doors, he wins a game of chess without so much as a stroke of his perma-stubbled chin. As particular sets of skills go, his are particularly particular, so who better to creep through the dingy hull and cranking air vents of the KMG Artemis in an effort to learn how the captain and crew are involved in the murder of Cole’s shipping tycoon boss, Tibu (Ramon Tikaram)?

Dealing death dressed in denim, Reed fights at close quarters, brief and brutal. His fists are hard and heavy as anchors, and he makes violent use of whatever objects are at hand — hook, padlock, harpoon — with nary a quip. “I wonder how many steaks I could make out of you?” the Stath mused in Crank ; “Do I look like a man who came halfway across Europe to die on a bridge?” he snarled in Transporter 3 . In Mutiny , he simply takes care of brutal business and there’s nothing fun about it, the tone prescribed by a grim plot-turn that’s only surprising in that Statham should choose to cover such similar ground to his last movie, A Working Man .

Viewers will probably have more fun than Reed does, but only just. For while Mutiny ’s adherence to back-to-basic, crunchy action is to be applauded, it often drags between fight sequences, with neither the conspiracy thread nor the characters, most of whom are disposable goons, engaging heart or mind. Even Reed teaming up with the third mate (Annabelle Wallis) only brings a dynamic that chugs like the boat’s engine. What’s odd is that Mutiny begins with a Leone-style close-up of Statham’s narrowed eyes, but any stylisation ends there. The next 90 minutes are all breezeblock-grey visuals, and a climactic scrap between a literal boatload of Marines, pirates, ex-military and ex-mercenary henchmen never threatens to be anything more than solid.
review_summary: A meat-and-potatoes action-thriller that sits heavy. Anyone who likes to have fun with the Stath might want to wait for next year’s Jason Statham Stole My Bike.

about_movie: In Luton, the friendship between two boys, Ish (Farhan Hasnat) and Maram (Yahya Kitana), is put to the test after a nasty run-in with the police.
review:
Writer-and-director Imran Perretta’s tender-hearted feature debut Ish is a coming-of-age story to rival (if not outrun) the likes of Scrapper and Aftersun . Like Lukas Dhont’s Close , the film — co-written by Disco Pigs ’ Enda Walsh —charts the rupture of the bond between two boys under societal pressure. In the sweet spot between sentimentality and restraint, it’s a striking, deeply moving study of how anger foments for young people facing systemic racism.

Set in a predominantly Muslim community in rundown Luton, the title belongs to 12-year-old Ishmail (an impressively nuanced performance from newcomer Farhan Hasnat), whose mother has recently passed away. While his family mourns, Ish seeks emotional refuge with his pal Maram (Yahya Kitana), a slightly more senior kid on the block. Together, they while away a rather bucolic summer: repurposing a dingy old mattress, building a den in the forest and staining their fingers foraging for blackberries.

Yet this blissful bubble is in danger of bursting. Maram is Palestinian, and intermittent radio reports from Gaza or about protests on British soil create an ambient backdrop of dread. Closer to home, there is a lurking threat, signalled by the very first shot, which lingers on an abandoned bike as invisible bystanders holler. Spliced throughout the film, footage from surveillance cameras — kitted out with facial-recognition tech — reveals that plainclothes police are constantly on their tail. And when the temperature rises to boiling point, Maram is literally snatched off the streets by stop-and-searchers while his terrified best bud flees.

Shot in a nostalgic, melancholic black-and-white by cinematographer Jermaine Canute Edwards, Ish expertly tempers a sense of adolescent hope with mounting grown-up pressures. Unsurprisingly, given that Perretta is also a composer, Jens Rosenlund Peterson and Nina Hartstone’s sound design — with its blaring planes, crackling radios and swelling orchestrals — effectively conveys the vast spectrum of emotion experienced by this teen duo. Nothing is overcooked in this hazy summer drama, which takes a complex look at rifts within working-class communities.
review_summary: Perretta’s impressive first feature is an intoxicating mix of weighty themes, unexpected beauty and teen euphoria, coalescing into a film that has a lot to say that you’ll want to savour.

movie_name: Original Title:Teenage Sex And Death At Camp Miasma
movie_name_try2: Teenage Sex And Death At Camp Miasma Review
about_movie: A filmmaker (Hannah Einbinder) working on the reboot of a slasher franchise is drawn to its reclusive star (Gillian Anderson).
review:
“If it gets too real, you can always turn it off, remember?” former actress Billy (Gillian Anderson) drawls seductively at shy filmmaker Kris (Hannah Einbinder), who’s finally ready to unburden herself of her most deviant fantasies. The same words appear on a poster for the video release of Camp Miasma, an ’80s slasher classic that spawned numerous awful sequels. Those words are both threatening and reassuring, a dare for the gore-curious and a promise of an escape route. But perhaps they also signal that to repress your deepest desires is its own kind of horror. Resist the impulse to turn it off. Keep watching. Become villain and victim. Stay alive.

As with their extraordinary film I Saw The TV Glow , writer-director Jane Schoenbrun wears their influences on their sleeve, from Friday The 13th to Videodrome via Mulholland Drive and Sunset Boulevard . But this time there’s more of a playfulness, as if, via Einbender’s obsessive cinephile Kris, Schoenbrun is teasing the audience for knowing what a split diopter looks like and smugly pointing it out to their movie-going companion (if you know, you know).

An introductory montage depicts the fictional Camp Miasma franchise via memorabilia, from VHS tapes to a wind-up toy of Little Death, the metal-box-headed killer. It’s an homage to schlocky horror that also affectionately skewers the over-intellectualisation of slashers, trash reevaluated by online discourses, ‘elevated horror’ and Hollywood remakes.

Kris, a queer indie darling stepping into the mainstream, has been tasked with resurrecting this “zombie IP”, as the cringey industry lingo goes. She meets Billy, the recluse who played the series’ original Final Girl but fell into obscurity, and is astounded to find Billy hasn’t left her grisly past behind. Instead she’s been living in the abandoned camp where Camp Miasma was shot, painting endless pictures that look exactly like Little Death’s face and evoke an old sexual trauma. “There’s a hole at the bottom of the lake where the movies come from,” she says. Little Death will rise again from that watery grave, an opening that pulses with golden light, with an insatiable bloodlust.

When Kris and Billy watch Camp Miasma together we’re transported into a gloriously silly pastiche of these formulaic but perversely appealing splatter-fests: irresponsible teens get drunk, hook up and get skewered by Little Death to an incongruous Counting Crows song. As much as Schoenbrun is clearly relishing the spectacle of geysers of cherry-coloured blood that are more absurd than disturbing, it’s not all frivolous fun. Little Death, played by I Saw The TV Glow ’s Jack Haven, earns a reveal midway through the film which radically shifts how we view the character. You don’t need to be a horror expert to recognise the filmmaker is reckoning with the complex legacy of transfeminine-coded horror villains such as Norman Bates, Leatherface and Angela, the killer from Sleepaway Camp, a cult favourite with an infamous transphobic reveal.

Little Death, of course, refers to la petite mort, the weakening of consciousness post-orgasm, and their metal ‘face’ resembles a camera. The deeply repressed Kris realises for her, sex, death and movies are one and the same, and there’s no greater thrill than watching and being watched. As she and Billy grow closer, she finds a path to liberation through the collapse of those boundaries, and Little Death draws nearer.

Miasma is a deliciously rich and cine-literate text, and to distil its innumerate references and layers of psychosexual meaning into a few words is a fool’s errand. Perhaps it would collapse under the weight of itself without its compelling and surprisingly tender lead performances, Einbinder concealing a profound loneliness beneath an uptight exterior and Anderson playing Billy with just the right degree of campy Southern Belle without losing a sense of her humanity. While I Saw The TV Glow used the iconography of ’90s TV to capture the isolation of denying your transgender identity, this is a more joyful, funny and literally visceral embrace of queerness and the strange, violent things that get us off.
review_summary: Everything is a remake of a remake, Schoenbrun tells us, but Miasma is an utterly unique, exhilaratingly entertaining vision, both blood-drenched and beautiful.

about_movie: After being destroyed by one too many ACME products in his pursuit of Roadrunner, Wile E. Coyote decides it’s time for the company to pay. Although he’s suing the biggest corporation in the world…
review:
Befitting its disaster-prone title character, Coyote Vs. Acme has faced many near-fatal obstacles in its path to cinemas. Originally set for release in 2023, by Warner Bros., it was shelved (for confusing tax reasons) and seemed destined for deletion, but was eventually sold to a new distributor. It’s an unpromising backstory. Yet, for once, Wile E. Coyote has emerged victorious. His film is no also-ran. It’s a work of unabashed chaotic comedy fun.

For over 75 years, Wile E. Coyote has devoted himself to catching the elusive Road Runner. Unable to compete in terms of speed, he employs a series of fantastical ACME-branded gadgets ­— rocket boots, giant magnets, a jet-propelled pogo stick — to help him snare the bird. They inevitably malfunction, blowing up Wile E. or sending him plummeting to the bottom of a ravine.

In Coyote Vs. Acme, after yet another foiled plan, Wile E. decides ACME is at fault. He’s going to sue the company for negligence, and he’s found just the wrong man to help him: Kevin Avery (Will Forte), a lazy, cheap lawyer who likes to settle cases quickly and is appalled at his new client’s silent determination. Where Coyote will stop at nothing to achieve his goals, Kevin believes you should try only until things start to get vaguely challenging.

It’s an enjoyably stupid set-up, logically ridiculous but somehow making perfect sense. Director Dave Green and screenwriter Samy Burch get this balance just right across the movie, taking a very similar approach to Who Framed Roger Rabbit, the Godfather of animation/live-action hybrids. It’s simply accepted that cartoon characters live among humans and the flesh-and-blood world is every bit as full of outsized villains with harebrained schemes, only theirs are more secretive and involve fewer anvils. Forte, often a very big comic actor, effectively plays the straight man to Wile E.’s silent madman. Their dynamic is well drawn, with a classic mismatched-buddy comedy arc. If the plotting in the final act gets a smidge muddled, leaning a little too much on formula, it never seems to matter too much.

For any Looney Tunes nerd, it’s a real treat to search the screen for innumerable Easter eggs. It goes so deep into the archives that it may leave the less Looney-attuned occasionally confused, wondering why Peter Lorre is ‘playing’ a scientist or why there’s an old lady chicken on a jury. But that respect for the viewer and love for the Looney Tunes world is what makes this movie work so well. It even feels edited to the same comic rhythms as a Looney Tunes short and, over its 100ish minutes, it maintains the same daffy joy.
review_summary: A daft, inventive, hilarious comedy that’s more than worth the wait. In Coyote Vs. Acme, it’s the audience that wins big.

about_movie: Raúl (Leonardo Sbaraglia) is a modern-day filmmaker struggling to finish his latest screenplay as he deals with the departure of his assistant Mónica (Aitana Sánchez-Gijón). Meanwhile, in Raúl’s 2004-set script, filmmaker Elsa (Bárbara Lennie) suffers migraines and tries to navigate complicated relationships.
review:
Pedro Almodóvar has explored his own profession before, in Antonio Banderas’ suffering filmmaker of Pain And Glory , for example. But there’s a sense of intense self-examination and even self-flagellation in his new film, as he looks at the tendency of artists to cannibalise the lives of those around them — to the detriment, perhaps, of their personal relationships.

Not that that’s immediately clear. We open in 2004 with a typical Almodóvarian heroine. Bárbara Lennie’s Elsa is a sometime filmmaker and commercials director who is afflicted with incapacitating migraines over the Christmas holidays. Her supportive boyfriend Bonifacio (Patrick Criado) is a firefighter/stripper who tries to nurse her through her affliction, as she recovers enough to reach out to friends like Patricia (Victoria Luengo), in crisis over her cheating husband, and Natalia (Milena Smit), a mother grieving for her son.

Quickly, however, we learn that Elsa is the creation of Raúl (Leonardo Sbaraglia), a filmmaker crafting his new script. He has his own problems: his assistant Mónica (Aitana Sánchez-Gijón) has to leave for personal reasons, so now he relies on his boyfriend Santi (Quim Gutiérrez). Shifts in Raúl’s life are reflected in Elsa’s story; he shapes her narrative, the god that determines her fate and that of everyone around her, so that the thrust of Elsa’s story shifts abruptly when he learns something new about one of his own loved ones.

Almodóvar films have frequently been metafictions and stories within stories, and it is in the interplay between reality and artifice that Almodóvar here explores the moral failings of… well, maybe himself, but certainly people like him. Raúl toys with his characters and cruelly exploits his friends in pursuit of a compelling story. The problem is that, like Almodóvar himself here, he hasn’t found a satisfying ending. Instead we have beautiful people in enviable apartments, having interesting conversations to no real end. It is no hardship to spend time with these characters, because Almodóvar’s faculty with dialogue remains undimmed. But this needed a stronger finish than simply pointing out an artist’s compromises along the way – even if the open-endedness does succeed in further blurring the lines between life and art.
review_summary: It’s a meandering and unfocused affair, touching on issues the director has explored before. But if you’re going to simply hang out with people, they might as well be Almodóvar characters.

about_movie: Lady Isabella (Sian Clifford), a lonely aristocrat with too much time and money on her hands, convinces a struggling director (Laurie Kynaston) to capture her every move. But her desire to be in the spotlight proves disastrous.
review:
After portraying the neurotic sister in Phoebe Waller-Bridge’s Fleabag , Sian Clifford serves up another dynamic performance on a silver platter as haughty aristocrat Lady  Isabella in Samuel Abrahams’ spirited debut feature. The mockumentary comedy follows Isabella, an eccentric 40-something woman living alone at the sprawling Ravenhyde Hall estate, who has tricked inquisitive director Sam (Laurie Kynaston) — no doubt loosely based on Abrahams — into believing that her marooned existence is worthy of documentation as she’s “aristocracy’s answer to the Kardashians”.

Shot like a low-budget fly-on-the-wall documentary, Lady ’s intriguing blend of mockumentary and surrealism matches the bizarrely engaging chemistry between Kynaston and Clifford, as a young director, vying for a candid study, clashes with a woman desperate to control her narrative. Clifford is particularly potent as Isabella, who in impassioned moments of pseudo-performance art (declaring that she’s the canvas, the paint and the brush) decides to compete in the annual talent show Stately Stars, which she hosts and judges for local children. As Abrahams’ sharp script, co-written with Miranda Campbell Bowling, reveals the reality of Isabella’s life, including dealing with menopause and struggling with grief, she begins to fade away, disappearing figuratively and literally in her gilded cage.

Jonny Woodley’s intensely haunting, vocally operatic score and Terri Higgins’ costume design (from a bright-azure tartan pantsuit to leopard print layered with a trench coat) add a psychedelic touch. While there are moments where the mockumentary format hiccups with the camera’s questionable positioning, and Clifford’s raucous performance tips into frenzied territory, Abrahams is quick to get the film back on track with moments of deep vulnerability. With shades of Saltburn ’s opulent aesthetic and Grey Gardens ’ ruminative loneliness, Lady embodies unexpectedly poignant ponderings on the invisibility of middle-aged women and the relationship between artist and muse.
review_summary: Sian Clifford is on top form in Samuel Abrahams’ debut, an engrossing study of invisible womanhood that plays out with bizarre hilarity and emotional sensitivity.

about_movie: His identity a secret once again, Spider-Man/Peter Parker (Holland) must take on a mysterious new threat which appears to take over people’s minds.
review:
Spider-Man has always been Marvel’s ace in the pack. Since his introduction in 1962, his comics have easily outsold rivals, and he has graduated to become the most consistently popular hero in the Marvel Cinematic Universe ; his last entry, No Way Home , earned just shy of $2 billion at the global box office, even in the pandemic. We can’t get enough of Ol’ Webhead, and for very obvious reasons: in a multiverse of wild and wacky superheroes and supervillains, Peter Parker is just a regular working-class kid from Queens, with great powers thrust upon him, trying his best.

This fourth solo entry, directed by Shang-Chi ’s Destin Daniel Cretton (series regular director Jon Watts previously stepped aside), tries hard not to forget that appeal. He’s not in high school any more, but Peter is still an ordinary New Yorker, diligently going to work every day. The opening 20 minutes of Brand New Day are the strongest of the film and among the best bit of mainstream superhero filmmaking in a long while: an extended montage showing our hero simply plugging away at what one character describes as “small potato stuff”.

Across multiple movies, guest appearances and Avengers team-ups it’s been vanishingly rare to see Spider-Man do the “friendly neighbourhood” part, and it is a genuine treat to see him beating up B-list baddies from his historic rogue’s gallery. This feels like the most comics-faithful entry so far, tactile and ground-level, while the addition of Jon Bernthal’s Frank Castle/Punisher as Peter’s sometime frenemy cements the New York-iness of it all, their hotheaded interactions bringing some lovely “I’m walking here!” energy to proceedings.

But Peter is lonely. As flashbacks from within the MCU logo remind us — the first time, perhaps, that a studio logo has been employed for “Previously on…” duties — the end of No Way Home saw Doctor Strange cast a spell that left everyone in the world with a case of amnesia as to who, exactly, was behind the mask. That’s left Peter feeling a serious case of heartache for his lost love MJ (Zendaya) and best bud/guy in the chair Ned (Jacob Batalon). The scenes between these three are among the most affecting of the film, with Zendaya finding the perfect pitch of poignancy and self-determination; while Batalon reminds us that Peter and Ned are just, at the heart of it, enormous nerds (shout out to a lovely Fellowship Of The Ring reference, the franchise crossover we never knew we wanted).

Tom Holland is brilliant in these moments. He has already more than proven that he can play all the shades of Peter — goofy, awkward, wise-cracking, emotional, ultimately decent — but here the glibness that characterised and sometimes undermined the series, and the MCU at large, is toned down. This is a less puppyish Peter, one battle-hardened and bruised by grief and solitude. Consequently, a new wrinkle is added; like the first Sam Raimi Spider-Man , it leans into the web-as-bodily-fluid, powers-as-puberty analogy. Think of it as an arachnid bar mitzvah: Peter is becoming a man. While the Tobey Maguire era executed the concept a little more successfully, it’s a nice enough idea. But it leads to the film’s first stumble, sending Peter searching for advice from Mark Ruffalo’s Bruce Banner, another Avenger who has had bodily changes.

All four Spider-Man films have had an assist from a top-level Avenger, and this one is no different — but you slightly wonder why. At this point, he is more famous than all of them, and the addition of the Hulk only slows things down, smashing not only buildings but also the narrative pace (which, for a two-and-a-half-hour film, counts for a lot). Even in a Spidey entry set entirely within the confines of the Five Boroughs, there are still major concessions being made to the wider universe. Which is a shame, because the mysterious nominal villain is spooky and well-played; to say who or what it is, exactly, would be giving too much away, but the effect is freaky and psychologically horrifying. And there are nice turns from Severance ’s Tramell Tillman (who, as Hollywood has correctly surmised, elevates everything he is in) and Stranger Things ’ Sadie Sink.

If the back half of the film feels a little sluggish, Cretton — who made his name with intimate dramas about young people like Short Term 12 — never fully loses focus of the guy behind the mask. Spider-Man is always at his best doing the friendly neighbourhood stuff, and when this film remembers that, we’re reminded why he’s still Marvel’s ace in the pack.
review_summary: A more mature, emotional and distinctly ground-level Spider-Man, Brand New Day doesn’t escape some of the usual MCU pitfalls but finds its heart in an earnest performance from Tom Holland.

about_movie: Dreaming of nautical adventure beyond her island, Moana (Catherine Laga'aia) teams up with demigod Maui (Dwayne Johnson) on a mission involving a magical stone.
review:
So. Here we are again, then. Back in the ’90s, Disney made a couple of live-action remakes of their animated classics, to modest success, but it wasn’t until 2010, when Tim Burton’s colourful live-action re-imagining of Alice In Wonderland earned a cool billion at the box office, that the Mouse House’s remake floodgates opened. Since then, we’ve had over 20 films adapting old, animated material into shiny live-action form — almost one a year. But few have felt so recent, or seemed so pointless, as Moana .

2016’s Moana , animated edition, is a high point in Walt Disney Animation Studios’ recent history: a fun, funny, poignant coming-of-age yarn with fantastic music and a winning Polynesian spin on the Disney Princess template. If you liked that film, so the thinking presumably goes, you’ll love this redo, a mere ten years later. Because it is, to all intents and purposes, exactly the same. It is Disney’s answer to Gus Van Sant’s Psycho : a shot-for-shot remake, an exercise purely in imitation.

Yet for all the familiarity, something feels off. It’s flat. To call it live action feels like a misnomer: a good two-thirds or so of this new film is animated, too. The live-action bits are simply the actors, comped in; even then, sometimes the actors are animated too, with clear use of digital doubles during some ocean sequences. (“This is a sacred place,” says one character at one point, of what is very plainly a green-screen studio.)

So crisp and sharp and coherent in the original, the animation here seems awkward and jarring, with goofy chicken Heihei and the blowdart-firing Kakamora keeping their cartoon aesthetic next to flesh-and-blood humans. The remake of Mulan , for all its faults, at least tried to ground its story in live action, excising elements that better suited the animated medium. There’s no attempt to actually adapt to the new medium here.

Catherine Laga'aia, replacing Auliʻi Cravalho as the new Moana, is a bright and breezy presence and has a Broadway-standard voice. Dwayne Johnson, reprising his role as the shapeshifting demigod Maui, sometimes feels a little like an AI interpretation of the character, uncanny in his nipple-less bodysuit and wig, but undeniably charismatic. And there are flashes where you forget the strangeness of the endeavour. Lin-Manuel Miranda’s songs, in particular, are unassailably brilliant, deserved earworms, with ancestor-tribute ‘We Know The Way’ proving particularly moving, especially when performed by a huge ensemble of Pacific Islander actors.

But it is all just very confusing. Where the original film felt vibrant and original, there seems to be no authorial voice detectable here. (It is directed by Hamilton ’s Thomas Kail, in his feature debut.) Even kids will feel shortchanged. Why would you want to pay money to watch a slightly worse version of the film you could watch on Disney+ ?
review_summary: A low point in Disney’s relentless live-action remake run. Make way, make way — for the original animated version instead.

about_movie: When Alice (Souheila Yacoub) loses her abusive husband (George Pullar) in a car accident, her personal hell is far from over: as he’s laid to rest, the Deadites come calling.
review:
The Evil Dead series is a tonal spectrum. The whole saga is oozing in entrails, but such ghoulish excesses are either deployed for splatstick laughs ( Evil Dead II , Army Of Darkness ) or genuine terror (Sam Raimi’s original The Evil Dead , Fede Alvarez’s 2013 Evil Dead ). The last outing of the cackling Deadite demons — Lee Cronin’s Evil Dead Rise — bridged the gap, combining raw gore and nasty shocks with a sense of Machiavellian mischief. Follow-up Evil Dead Burn , from incoming director Sébastian Vaniček, cranks the dial even darker, with nerve-rattling results.

Impressively, Vaniček — with co-writer Florent Bernard — manages to shake up the formula a little. How the Kandarian nasties get involved is different to any other film in the series. And for the first time, the Deadites have a purpose beyond simply swallowing souls — they’re on the backfoot, and they’re pissed. That makes them even deadlier for Alice (a hard-as-nails Souheila Yacoub), trying to tough out an emotional afternoon with the in-laws, hiding from them that their recently deceased son Will — her husband — was an angry, violent man; a dramatically rich dynamic for the demons to mine once they start infecting the family one by one.

Vaniček revels in the possibilities provided by an Evil Dead movie. A deeply stylish director, he orchestrates chaotic extended takes and gravity-defying tracking shots with thrilling precision. And he gets seriously gory, too — smashing heads, slamming fingers in doors, and melting charred flesh like pulled pork. There is a fire, an anger here that permeates the film, evident both in the human characters — Will’s propensity for violence is evidently an inherited family trait, simmering in dad Edgar (Erroll Shand), and latent deep within son Joseph ( Wednesday ’s Hunter Doohan) — and the supernatural forces.

But even for hardened Evil Dead fans, it’s a gruelling ride. The series exists on a tonal knife-edge between gleeful nastiness and the just plain unpleasant — and Burn occasionally strays on the wrong side of it. While the film has a genuine sense of humour, it’s also an intentionally dark and dour exploration of male aggression, set in the depths of winter, amid the ashes of grief. Combine that with this level of bloodshed, and it’s a lot to stomach. Oddly, it’s a little slack on the pacing side too. For all Vaniček clearly understands Evil Dead’s ferocious kineticism, he favours a series of slow build-ups (and gut-churning pay-offs) rather than letting the mayhem rocket along.

Still, this is a bold and brutal entry that refuses to water down its themes or its gnarliness, with smart twists on series lore. Maybe a little more grooviness next time, though.
review_summary: The darkest Evil Dead yet is sure to be an acquired taste — but there is incredible craft here, along with plenty of guts (of all kinds).

movie_name_try2: In The Hand Of Dante Review
about_movie: In the early 2000s, writer Nick Tosches (Oscar Isaac) is hired by a Mafia don to verify and steal an original copy of ‘The Divine Comedy’ by Dante Alighieri. In 14th-century Florence, Dante (also Isaac) grapples with the creation of his greatest work.
review:
This is a bizarre misfire from director Julian Schnabel. His previous work — locked-in-syndrome POV drama The Diving Bell And The Butterfly ; Vincent van Gogh biopic At Eternity’s Gate — achieved something far more profound. In The Hand Of Dante , meanwhile, is almost impressively pretentious and misjudged at almost every turn.

Set across twin timelines, it sees Oscar Isaac play both 14-century poet Dante Alighieri, of ‘Divine Comedy’ fame, and real-life New York “literary iconoclast” Nick Tosches. (The modern-day side is shot in crisp black-and-white, while the flashbacks are in Horrible Histories colour.) The film adapts Tosches’ 2002 sprawling, ambitious book of the same name, which included Tosches himself as a semifictional protagonist. In the modern day, Tosches accepts a job from an old friend, to steal a rare copy of Dante’s ‘The Divine Comedy’, bringing him into orbit with the Mafia; in the 1300s, Dante wrestles with his spiritual and artistic practice, via unintentionally comic levels of pomposity.

Taking a Cloud Atlas approach to casting, we see several actors take on dual roles in both timelines, including Gal Gadot, Louis Cancelmi and Gerard Butler, the last as both a nastily murderous Mob enforcer and the Pope. Also, Martin Scorsese pops by with a massive beard for a confusing cameo as Dante’s mentor. It’s not nearly as fun as any of that sounds. Everyone is dreadfully miscast, almost entirely across the board, while Schnabel’s tone and approach is both overly self-important and fatally confused about whatever it is trying to say.

The intention, perhaps, was to make something on a par with epic Renaissance-era poetry — a pompous, metafictional piece of art, about art — but while occasionally pretty, it is mainly just overlong and boring. “My books can’t be edited any more than a leopard can be manicured,” insists Nick at the beginning of the film; perhaps Schnabel should have considered editing this two-and-a-half hour folly into something even remotely watchable.
review_summary: Kind of a disaster. Not quite the seventh circle of hell — but it’s dangerously close.

about_movie: Jill (Zoey Deutch) is an aspiring baker who leaves voicemails for her dead sister detailing her chaotic life in San Francisco. Wes (Nick Robinson) is a Texan real-estate agent whose new work phone is receiving Jill’s tell-all missives. Sparks soon fly.
review:
The romcom renaissance is upon us. It started unassumingly enough, a Rye Lane here and an Anyone But You there. But in the last couple of months alone we’ve had Finding Emily and Office Romance , and now writer-director Leah McKendrick’s lovely Netflix warm-and-fuzzies-triggerer Voicemails For Isabelle (aka You’ve Got Voicemail ) comes along. And honestly, not a moment too soon. It seems at a time where it’s become so easy to see nothing but war, hate and division in our everyday lives, the humble romantic comedy has returned to allow us an escape into a world where joy, love and connection are still possible… where meets can be cute, ethical quandaries can be quashed by good intentions, everyone dances to Robyn, and Nick Robinson remains forever young.

The set-up for McKendrick’s sophomore feature, which follows the multi-hyphenate’s self-starring 2023 directorial debut Scrambled , is, it must be said, more than a little eyebrow-raising on the face of it. Zoey Deutch stars as Jill, an up-and-coming baker living in San Francisco who — when not being subjected to the workplace outbursts of her pompous boss Chef Bastien (a dependably chuckle-worthy Nick Offerman) or the bedroom outbursts of her latest dates — is relaying said encounters to her cystic fibrosis-stricken sister Isabelle over voicemail. When tragedy — and an unfortunate reassigned number — strikes, however, doe-eyed Texan real-estate agent Wes (the aforementioned, ever-youthful Robinson) finds himself receiving Jill’s confessional recordings.

Now because this is a romcom, which is time and again a realm reserved exclusively for irrational decision-makers, rather than disconnecting the phone and carrying on with his life, Wes finds himself invested in Jill’s love life, before long landing himself in San Fran to set up a (digitally aided-and-abetted) date with destiny. Which, as you can probably figure out, is a great idea — until it’s really not a great idea.

The thing about Voicemails For Isabelle is that yes , its set-up is perhaps just a little bit icky. And yes , there are at least a dozen occasions where you can’t help but think hair-sweeping, mild-mannered would-be lothario Wes could do himself — and Jill — a lot of favours by just fessing up to the whole voicemail thing that obviously has to come out sooner or later. And also yes , just because Will’s lovable soon-to-be-wed pals Andy (Harry Shum Jr.) and Breeda (McKendrick) repeatedly remind him what he’s doing is giving big red-flag energy, that doesn’t make it any less iffy. But here’s the thing: the second Wes and Jill meet, you just won’t care about any of that anymore.

As soon as Deutch and Robinson share the frame — the movie’s Tom Hanks and Meg Ryan aspirations literally spelled out for us, although McKendrick’s alternately zinger-filled and touching writing so winningly evokes Nora Ephron that overt references to her movie, while cute, really aren’t needed at all — the atavistic desire to see these two together, to stay plugged into the terawatt electricity surging through every one of his winsome, Love, Simon honed looks and every one of her ear-to-ear, bulb-bright smiles, overrides all logic systems. And as the duo inevitably fall for one another, their open wounds healing just a little more with each bus tour they take and eminently nommable-looking pud they share — his sensitivity and her strength pulling them both out of the dark, allowing them to let down their walls — the film opens up, goes deep (steady on!), and becomes something entirely its own. Be prepared for the best “eating something and instantly being taken back to a very poignant childhood memory” scene this side of Ratatouille , and an exquisitely deployed needle drop of deep-cut Taylor Swift ballad 'Marjorie' that keys into the film's emotional frequency almost preternaturally well.

As a romcom with a wacky premise, Voicemails For Isabelle is charming, and sweet, and lovely enough as it is. But as the story of two wayward souls who’ve been searching for their loved-ones-lost in all they see and do for so long that the possibility of embracing new love — of letting the love that shaped them help make something new, free of guilt — is as terrifying as it is exciting, this has levels to it that you forget the cosy trappings of the genre can create space for. That Leah McKendrick has been able to make something like this, that’s also sex-positive, also feminist in its formulation, and also manages to be both romantic and comedic in roughly equal measure is incredibly refreshing. And frankly, any movie that factors a flash-mob dance-along to Robyn’s ‘Dancing On My Own’ into its emotional climax is already a must-see. So, what are you waiting for?
review_summary: The romcom comeback is well and truly on — and Voicemails For Isabelle leads the way. Nick Robinson and Zoey Deutch’s palpable on-screen chemistry is enough to make even the coldest of hearts believe in love.

about_movie: When their house is mysteriously sealed in by unnatural-looking rain, the Delgado family are forced to survive with their diminishing resources — and face an unseen threat outside.
review:
The Last House begins with a quote from Arthur C. Clarke, one of the great forefathers of modern science-fiction: “How inappropriate to call this planet Earth when it is clearly Ocean.” It’s a bold name to invoke. It goes without saying that this particular science-fiction does not, in fact, come near to scraping the giddy heights of the Clarke adaptation 2001: A Space Odyssey . Instead, it’s a relatively cheap-and-cheerful straight-to-streaming affair, largely inoffensive if ultimately unmemorable.

If you can look past the slightly stodgy voiceover which introduces things — “The day the rain came, we learned we were not alone…” — there is a decent-enough premise to wrestle with here. After an unnatural spell of precipitation, the Delgado family — mum Ann (Greta Lee), dad Jason (Wagner Moura), daughter Ruth (Riley Chung) and son Graham (Noah Alexander Sosnowski) — find themselves trapped in their suburban house. The doors and windows are sealed shut, with no chance of escape. And it seems like the baffling phenomenon is happening to everyone, their neighbours in a similar predicament.

At first, they try not to panic, try to make the best of a bad situation, and there is a nice pandemic-tinged narrative thread, in seeking pockets of joy amid a confusing misery. Like the recent Julia Roberts film Leave The World Behind , it’s an apocalyptic streaming film that slightly ironically acts as an ode to physical media: the family watch DVDs, listen to music on vinyl and play board games, finding — as with the first Covid lockdown — something wholesome about enforced confinement in the shadow of horror.

Moura and Lee are perhaps best known for their work in films aching with nuance ( The Secret Agent and Past Lives , respectively). This film, with the greatest will in the world, lacks that quality. But they do good, committed work in spite of an occasionally ropey script and clichéd dialogue (“What the hell is going on?”). It is about what you might expect from French director Louis Leterrier, a filmmaker best known for Jason Statham’s Transporter series, whose last movie ( Fast X ) saw a car destroy two helicopters at once in mid-air.

This is certainly a more contained film than those silly actioners, being limited entirely to the walls of the family home, and there is some fun and ingenuity to be had in the problem-solving that arises when forced to live off only what is inside your gaff. Where it slightly goes off the boil is in the third act, when the human-level drama gives way to computer-generated tentacle monsters and more outlandish silliness besides. Arthur C. Clarke this ain’t, but as a modestly diverting couple of hours it’s a perfectly good time: some solid showers, rather than a perfect storm.
review_summary: Netflix’s latest attempt at the next Bird Box — a mysterious apocalyptic sci-fi to generate some watercooler buzz — doesn’t fully utilise its acting talents, but the premise is fun enough to justify itself.

movie_name: Original Title:Insidious: Out Of The Further
movie_name_try2: Insidious: Out Of The Further Review
about_movie: Gemma and her daughter Maya are besieged by a powerful and insatiable entity from The Further who, along with his acolytes, plans to use its unique powers to open a door to the other side and bring a hoard of spirits and demons through to take over the real world.
review:
The Insidious franchise has been treating audiences to various thrill rides for over 15 years at this point, and with the Lamberts finally getting closure (literally) in 2023’s The Red Door , it’s time for The Further to unleash fresh horror onto a new, unsuspecting family.

Enter Amelia Eve’s Gemma, a young mother still living in her childhood home and clinging to the trauma that shaped her. She’s raising her daughter Maya (Island Austin), holding down a solid job, and dating a handsome cop (Brandon Perea). Naturally, their fragile peace doesn’t last: it’s soon shattered by a supernatural nightmare bleeding straight out of The Further.

Director Jacob Chase creates some atmospheric set-pieces that feel tangible in their terror, and delivers the well-crafted jump scares that Insidious fans have come to expect. There are definitely moments here that rival the iconic shock of the Lipstick-face Demon from the first film, but there's more devious dread here too. A pillow‑fort sequence is a standout — all panicked claustrophobia and spooky peeking faces — and for anyone who suffers from odontophobia, let's just say that Gemma's career as a dental hygienist garners plenty of opportunities to set your teeth on edge.

Sam Spruell’s big bad brings convincing menace, and his three earthbound disciples add decent sideshow creepiness, even if they lean heavily on the tired ‘old people are gross’ trope. Unfortunately, the clichés don’t stop there: Maisie Richardson‑Sellers’ Clare is saddled with the lazy ‘magical negro’ archetype, and is given fairly short shrift, including a baffling heist-planning scene involving a punnet of tattooed grapefruits.

Still, the performances are solid across the board, and it’s always a pleasure to have Lin Shaye back as Elise – the franchise’s stalwart paranormal investigator – now offering guidance from the other side.

Insidious: Out Of The Further doesn’t reinvent the franchise, but when it leans into its eerie set‑pieces and fresh family dynamic, it delivers exactly the kind of polished, popcorn‑friendly terror that fans come for.
review_summary: The Insidious films may have offered diminishing returns since the original, but Out Of The Further is a decent instalment packing some hair-raising scares.

movie_name: Original Title:The End Of Oak Street
movie_name_try2: The End Of Oak Street Review
about_movie: After a mysterious portal transports their town to a prehistoric era filled with deadly dinosaurs, the Platt family must do everything they can to survive.
review:
Has anyone had as strange or circuitous a career as David Robert Mitchell? The American filmmaker started out with 2010’s hazy teen drama The Myth Of The American Sleepover , broke out with 2014’s cult hit horror It Follows , and then took a sharp left-turn into surreal neo-noir thrills with 2018’s Under The Silver Lake (which featured a nude owl-woman, a random skunk, a mysterious pirate, and a bit where Andrew Garfield shoves an egg into a child’s mouth). Now this former indie darling takes a swerve into summer-blockbuster territory with The End Of Oak Street , a film that wholeheartedly embraces its big, brash genre pleasures.

This is 1982: a suburban America of Polaroids and perms, picket fences and playdates. It’s here we meet the Platts, a seemingly perfect nuclear family, soundtracked by Michael Giacchino’s sweeping, John Williams-esque score. Under the surface, however, all is not well: dad Greg (Ewan McGregor) has lost his job and has started drinking, mum Denise (Anne Hathaway) is a frustrated writer, son Brian (Christian Convery) is secretly smoking, and daughter Audrey (Maisy Stella) is worrying her parents will divorce, while very saliently quoting Carl Sagan.

As if that weren’t enough to be dealing with, strange prehistoric plants begin cropping up in the neighbourhood, and before they know it, the entire town has been mysteriously transported back in time, to when dinosaurs — those with paleontologically accurate feathers and fur, please note — roamed the earth.

If you were thinking this sounds a bit like a suburban Jurassic Park (‘Jurassic Park Crescent’?), you’re not far off. Mitchell wears his Spielberg influences on his sleeve, from the shots of kids riding bikes, to the fractious family unit, to the close encounters with bright light, to the T-Rex earning top billing. There’s even one big pile of shit. Sneakily, Mitchell has made a Jurassic -coded dino-movie which largely out-dinos a lot of the recent Jurassic entries , chock-full of deliciously tense set-pieces. It’s mounted robustly and handsomely, too. Like the New Hollywood auteurs of old, the cinematography deploys careful, deliberate framing and some very prominent split-diopter shots; if it weren’t for all the (excellent) CGI, it could pass for a 1980s period piece.

Which is not to say it isn’t supremely daft. How and why the dinosaurs arrive is never explained, the film fairly hoping you will enjoy the tense fun on its own silly terms, its internal logic hardly standing up to too much scrutiny. The Platts make some terrible decisions, too (going on a suicidal rescue mission for a dog, jumping off a roof, walloping a T-Rex with a small hammer). But it is, ultimately, the convincing character work that makes this outlandish trip such a delight: suburban anxiety, played out through the Cretaceous period.
review_summary: Mitchell makes for one of the better Spielberg tribute acts in recent memory. Your inner seven-year-old will have a great time.

about_movie: Shy princess Saira (voiced by Shabana Azeez) must venture across the galaxy to rescue her ex-girlfriend from the Straight White Maliens.
review:
“She’s a lesbian, she’s in space, and she’s also a princess (oh, and she’s very sad!),” trills a musical interlude over this very Australian for-adults-only animated adventure’s title card. And if that sounds endearing as opposed to toe-curling, this candy-coloured inter-gay-lactic voyage, clearly inspired by Rick And Morty and streaming service Adult Swim, might be for you.

Princess Saira (voiced by The Pitt ’s Shabana Azeez) is the painfully insecure daughter of the two queens of queer planet Clitopolis (“famously hard to find!”). Overshadowed by her uncaring but universally adored mums, incapable of summoning her “labrys” (her destined all-powerful lesbian weapon), and dumped by her super-hot bounty-hunter girlfriend Kiki The Destroyer (Bernie Van Tiel), things are looking pretty bleak. Early on, first-time filmmakers and IRL couple Leela Varghese and Emma Hough Hobbs launch into a hilarious homage to The Twilight Saga: New Moon ’s break-up montage, with Saira staring glumly out of a window to a funereal soundtrack and screaming into a pillow à la Bella Swan having been ditched by Edward Cullen.

But the film’s funniest moments mostly, and unfortunately, come from the Straight White Maliens, a trio of incel extraterrestrials who kidnap Kiki and lure Saira into handing over her labrys to power their Hot Chick Magnet, obviously. Voiced by the comedy trio Aunty Donna, they’re a brilliant marriage of performance and character design, resembling strips of blinding-white gum with permanently petulant blue eyebrows. There’s a refreshing looseness to their scenes as they ineptly role-play approaching women in bars (“I wore a nice shirt to this bar”, “It’s making me horny”), and over-explain the rules of a RPG featuring a character named Big Titty Sorcerer.

It’s a bit of a shame the same can’t be said of all the stabs at humour, which often feel dated and overly safe, relying too heavily on stereotypes or tired gags about monstrous penises. As Saira journeys across space in search of both her labrys and Kiki, she encounters various quirky characters, from a sentient problematic spaceship (a fun turn by Richard Roxburgh) who acts like an Aussie lorry driver, to drag royalty Blade (Kween Kong) and upbeat singer-songwriter Willow (Gemma Chua-Tran). It’s all rather hit-and-miss, and your mileage may also vary with some of the cutesy musical sequences.

And yet despite its flaws, it’s hard not to be charmed by this scrappy, deeply silly sex-positive sci-fi fantasy. Saira’s true mission, to overcome her literally monstrous self-doubt and love herself without a super-hot girlfriend, feels like a timeless one, and will undoubtedly resonate with LGBTQ+ audiences.
review_summary: Unchallenging and sometimes clichéd but ultimately good queer fun,this just about balances zany humour with earnestness, boosted by terrific comic creations the Straight White Maliens.

about_movie: On the one night of the year premarital sex is legal, newly single Owen (Callum Turner) meets hopeless romantic Allie (Monica Barbaro).
review:
The elevator pitch for One Night Only probably read “ The Purge , but for one-night stands.” It’s a promise it lives up to in all the wrong ways. The first Purge movie — in which crime is legal one night a year — was a bog-standard home-invasion thriller. Similarly, One Night Only could have unfolded on a regular holiday (Valentine’s Day, perhaps, or even Halloween) without much changing by way of plot. That it features such a bizarre, half-baked idea driving it, however, is morbidly fascinating.

Romcom connoisseur Will Gluck ( Friends With Benefits , Anyone But You ) transposes the genre’s tropes into an odd quasi-dystopia, a world where non-married couples are barred from sex for 364 days of the year. As the clock counts down to a night of state-sanctioned debauchery, newly single New Yorker Owen (Callum Turner) searches for a sexual partner. A comedy of errors has him bumping repeatedly into Allie (Monica Barbaro), a woman on the lookout for her special someone, whose imaginative daydreams are about the only times the film gets funny or saucy. The appealing duo share physical chemistry, but don’t click emotionally at first. You know the rest. But given its audacious premise, One Night Only shouldn’t be so predictable.

Gluck’s awkward mapping of a traditional romcom onto a high concept more befitting of a political thriller leads to characters shedding all recognisable human traits. The backdrop is one of control, robbing people of the power of choice. But the movie’s strangely slapdash approach embodies that very same conservatism, which makes things a whole lot less fun and sensual. The narrative rests on happenstance, stripping Owen and Allie of active decision-making. This yields a film of emotional and sexual passivity, when it ought to feel explosively charged.

The premise would be easy enough to hand-wave were it a mere background detail, rather than a distracting centrepiece. Each exchange dovetails into exposition meant to convince us of a world that just doesn’t fit together, even with its amusing array of “one night”-themed advertising on every street corner. Perhaps the creative energy spent on in-world billboards would have been better deployed elsewhere — like ensuring Turner and Barbaro shared enough screen time. It takes about an hour for Owen and Allie to have a real conversation.

As the pair help each other navigate the evening, their banter flows naturally enough, but often ends in flailing punchlines. The humour, like the drama, rarely stems from a coherent sense of character or setting. Despite the actors’ best efforts to conjure sparks, they’re at the mercy of a tale that insists that this world is a functional satire of either fascism or social prudishness (take your pick). In the end, One Night Only submits to the oppressive forces it purports to reject, robbing its characters and viewers alike of the raucous good time promised by its ticking clock.
review_summary: One Night Only places attractive, likable stars in a world where neither the people nor the politics make much sense. It’s rare for a romcom to be this un-exciting.

about_movie: For their apparently final feature-length outing, Johnny Knoxville and his ragtag crew create new skits in which to inflict pain upon each other. They also look back at their favourite Jackass stunts from more than 25 years, and reveal unseen sketches.
review:
A fearless and occasionally feckless bunch of pranksters and would-be-stuntmen (the solo woman here, Rachel Wolfson, doesn’t perform any pranks in this fifth film outing), the Jackass mob have been egging each other on to perform wincingly painful tricks since the turn of the millennium.

Series co-creator Johnny Knoxville and the rest of his (increasingly ageing) team know they can’t really continue thrashing their bodies and testing their physical resilience in unpleasant ways — as much fun as they’re all still having. When we see them getting slammed in the nuts, injected and Tasered, it remains riotously funny, but it’s also like watching Tom Cruise repeatedly defy death in the later Mission: Impossible films: hugely impressive, but enough to make you beg them to stop, for the love of God, before all this insanity kills them.

Those hoping for fresh insanity here may be disappointed; less than an hour of Best And Last ’s 92 minutes are dedicated to brand-new stunts. A typical new entry involves Steve-O, Jackass ’ most prominent survivor other than Knoxville, receiving a forceful prostate exam from a robot, its metal fingers lubed up with peanut butter. It is a disgusting, extremely uncomfortable scene that will have all but the must stoic viewer laughing to the verge of tears. Of the old clips resurfaced, meanwhile, many will gasp at Ryan Dunn inserting a toy car in his anus, or cheer as Knoxville rides a rocket into the air and crashes into a lake.

In one previously unseen clip, which MTV refused to broadcast on the TV series, Knoxville — convincingly dressed as an escaped convict — hacksaws his way through handcuffs in a hardware store and gets arrested. It’s a typically audacious and utterly idiotic stunt, which escalates dramatically when the LAPD turn up, guns drawn. But then, thinking things through has never really been the point of Jackass . And that’s part of its appeal, too. If this truly is goodbye, it feels dumbly fitting.
review_summary: Part greatest hits compilation, this is fun and peppered with fresh prankery. A fine way to sign off for the smashed groins and punctured bums of America’s gross-out kings on their last big-screen blow-out.

about_movie: The Mandalorian bounty hunter Din Djarin (Pedro Pascal) and his apprentice Grogu are tasked by the New Republic to rescue Rotta The Hutt (Jeremy Allen White) from captivity.
review:
A long time ago, in a galaxy far, far away — specifically, November 2019 — Pedro Pascal’s Din Djarin first stepped into a seedy cantina in the Outer Rim. Set during the fragile peace of the Star Wars ’ New Republic era — the Weimar-esque interwar years, post-Vader, pre-Ren — The Mandalorian was an unusual offering. Star Wars’ first foray into live-action TV (notwithstanding the Star Wars Holiday Special or Ewoks: The Battle For Endor ), this was a series with no major star, no legacy characters, no lightsabers.

That feels like a long time ago. Legacy characters and sabers (dark or otherwise) have since snuck their way into the series, while Pedro Pascal’s profile has risen faster than the Millennium Falcon bombing it down the Kessel Run. The show’s scope and scale was never small, so it makes sense that Mando and Grogu have found their way to the big screen; still, the series seemed to find a natural conclusion at the end of Season 2 , when Din tearfully left his little green mate in the capable hands of one L. Skywalker. Since then, it’s felt a little like treading water, with a third season that introduced lots more Mandalorians but fewer compelling stories. That feeling isn’t entirely shaken off in this feature-length tale, which doesn’t add much to the canon.

Instead, it’s a back-to-basics adventure, obeying the founding principles of the show: blending elements of Westerns and old Saturday-morning one-reels into a ripping-yarn caper, while studiously avoiding getting bogged down in complex lore or anything too deep. It begins confidently in this manner, with Mando — introduced heroically in the shadows — engaging in some satisfying gun-slinging and cowboyish drawls (“I can bring you in warm, or I can bring you in cold,” he snarls, nodding to the pilot episode.)

The first half of the film rattles along at a merry old pace with some stirring action, and characters both old ( Star Wars Rebels ’ furry blue pilot Zeb, voiced by Steve Blum, makes his film debut here) and new (Sigourney Weaver adds another nerd notch to her CV as Colonel Ward) peppering the background. Mando is now working full time as an “independent contractor” for the New Republic: still a bounty hunter for hire, but exclusively for the good guys. This is how he enters the orbit of the Twins, the Hutt gangsters desperate to retrieve their roided-up nephew Rotta ( voiced by Jeremy Allen White ), son of the fearsome Jabba.

Rotta is the film’s first stumble: while the twins speak in traditional tongue-twisting Huttese, Rotta bafflingly speaks Galactic Basic with a New York accent, with which he whines about being a nepo baby (nepo-Jabb-y?) while getting a droid-based sports massage. Rotta might be a fan-favourite from his appearance in the original Clone Wars film , but here his presence begins to make the film feel repetitive — quite literally, sluggish. Time and time again, Mando is forced to fight reams of CGI aliens where the stakes rarely rise above, “How is Mando going to get out of this pickle?”

Just when you think the film has forgotten the second character named in its title, the pace abruptly slows in the third act, when Mando takes a backseat to the Artist Formerly Known As Baby Yoda. There is a lovely, bucolic, near-wordless sequence in which Grogu takes the lead, demonstrating quiet tenderness, resilience and leadership that belies his mere 50-something years. While the film sometimes coasts on his cuteness — the introduction of multiple equally adorable Anzellans adds to this feeling — it never forgets that he remains its greatest asset.

What it does slightly forget to do, though, is move the story forward in any meaningful way. Oddly, it feels like the least consequential Mandalorian chapter yet, with previous episodes from the TV incarnation — or even segments of the much-maligned Book Of Boba Fett — having more impact on the narrative. It’s thinner than skimmed blue milk, with longtime series stewards Jon Favreau (director and co-writer) and Dave Filoni (co-writer and new Galactic Emperor of the entire franchise ) largely playing it safe. Perhaps after the relative disappointment of The Rise Of Skywalker , this is all it needed or was intended to be. The Mandalorian And Grogu is, primarily, For Kids, as George Lucas always insisted Star Wars was, and on those modest terms, it finds the way.
review_summary: The first Star Wars film in nearly a decade doesn’t shake up the formula: instead, it’s a lively if inessential extended episode of the series. But Mando remains cool, and Grogu remains cute
